Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Two hepatic metastases (2.2 cm in segment II, 3 cm in segment V) are solitary, ≤5 cm each, and located in segments that allow parenchymal‑sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant.  
  • No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
  • RAS wild‑type and MSS status do not affect surgical resectability.  
  • Patient has no significant comorbidities, suggesting sufficient physiologic reserve for major abdominal surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Urgent left‑sided colon resection (segmental colectomy or left hemicolectomy) to relieve obstruction and obtain oncologic control of the primary tumor.  
   – Rationale: Symptomatic primary lesion is the immediate priority; resection also provides pathological staging and eliminates a source of future complications.  

B. After postoperative recovery (typically 2–4 weeks), perform staged liver‑directed surgery: anatomic or non‑anatomic segmentectomy of segment II and segment V (or combined limited hepatectomy) preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.  
   – Rationale: Staged approach allows assessment of postoperative hepatic function and ensures safe margin attainment; lesions are amenable to curative‑intent resection with clear margins (R0).  

C. Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± cetuximab given RAS wild‑type) initiated within 6–8 weeks after liver surgery.  
   – Rationale: High pre‑operative CEA (120 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology; adjuvant therapy reduces recurrence risk.  

D. Surveillance protocol: CEA every 3 months for 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months, colonoscopy at 1 year.  
   – Rationale: Early detection of recurrence or new metastases improves long‑term outcomes.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance (Minagawa et al.)

MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (curative intent)  
- Rationale:  
  • Single hepatic lesion, 2.5 cm, peripheral (segment VI) – amenable to wedge resection or segmentectomy with adequate margins.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on FDG‑PET; solitary extra‑hepatic site absent.  
  • Primary tumor confined to right colon (ileocecal region) without radiologic evidence of adjacent organ invasion.  
  • Expected future liver remnant >30 % after limited resection; no underlying liver disease reported.  
  • Patient age (56) and presumed adequate performance status support operative tolerance.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Colonoscopy with biopsy confirmation, endoscopic tattooing of the tumor for intra‑operative localization.  
   – Baseline labs: liver function panel, coagulation profile, CEA trend, KRAS status already known.  
   – Cardiopulmonary assessment (e.g., ECG, echocardiogram, pulmonary function if indicated).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional but preferred)  
   – 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) given the KRAS‑mutated, CEA‑elevated disease to address micrometastatic burden and assess tumor biology.  
   – Re‑staging CT/MRI after chemotherapy to confirm stability or response of the liver lesion and exclude new sites.  

C. Surgical resection (simultaneous approach)  
   – Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy for the primary tumor.  
   – Anatomical segment VI resection (segmentectomy) or non‑anatomic wedge resection achieving ≥1 cm margin, performed during the same operation.  
   – Rationale: limited hepatic disease, peripheral location, and low operative morbidity allow a single‑stage procedure, reducing overall treatment time and hospitalizations.  

D. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   – Completion of a total of 6 months peri‑operative chemotherapy (additional 2–3 cycles post‑op if neoadjuvant given).  
   – Surveillance plan: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline between clearly resectable and requiring optimization).  
- Rationale:  
   Liver lesion: solitary 1.8 cm metastasis in segment III, amenable to limited anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with preservation of a sufficient future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver).  
   Primary tumor: T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with limited parietal invasion; no circumferential resection margin (CRM) involvement on MRI, making sphincter‑preserving resection feasible.  
   No documented extra‑hepatic disease; CEA elevated but not a contraindication.  
   Patient age 68, smoking history only; assuming adequate performance status and liver function, combined or staged resection is technically possible.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) to the rectum – to achieve local tumor down‑staging while minimizing treatment delay for the liver lesion.  
B. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3–4 cycles FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS wild‑type) – to treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially further shrink the liver metastasis if needed.  
C. Surgical resection (simultaneous approach) – perform low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision together with a wedge/segmental resection of segment III. Rationale: small peripheral liver lesion allows safe concurrent resection, reduces overall treatment time, and avoids two separate major operations.  
D. Adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of peri‑operative chemotherapy to a total of 6–8 cycles) – to consolidate response and address any residual microscopic disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
(Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Three hepatic lesions, each ≤3 cm, fulfilling the “≤5 lesions ≤5 cm” criterion for resection.  
  • Lesions located in segments IV, V, and VI allow either parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomies or an extended right hepatectomy with preservation of left lateral sectors (II‑III), providing an anticipated future liver remnant ≥30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver.  
  • Imaging shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no radiologic invasion, indicating that vascular resection is not mandatory.  
  • No reported extra‑hepatic disease; CEA is markedly elevated but does not preclude resection.  
  • KRAS mutation and BRAF wild‑type status do not affect technical resectability.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab)  
   – Rationale: treat micrometastatic disease, potentially down‑size lesions, and assess tumor biology; high CEA suggests aggressive disease.  

B. Restaging after chemotherapy (contrast‑enhanced CT and liver MRI with volumetry)  
   – Rationale: confirm continued resectability, quantify FLR, and detect any new extra‑hepatic sites.  

C. Surgical phase (choice based on patient fitness and FLR assessment)  
   • If FLR ≥30 % and patient has good performance status: simultaneous colon resection (segmental colectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy) and liver resection (parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomies of IV, V, VI or extended right hepatectomy).  
   • If concerns about postoperative hepatic insufficiency or comorbidity: staged approach – first colon resection, then liver resection 4–6 weeks later after recovery.  

D. Post‑operative systemic therapy to complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy  
   – Rationale: consolidate response, reduce recurrence risk; consider continuation of the same regimen used pre‑operatively.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Four peripheral hepatic lesions ≤3 cm located in segments II, III, V, and VIII, without major vascular invasion, meet criteria for hepatic resection with curative intent.  
  • Absence of extra‑hepatic disease on imaging supports a curative approach.  
  • The distribution involves both lobes; while technically resectable, the need to preserve an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) may require volumetric assessment or staged strategy, thus the “potentially” qualifier.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 cycles FOLFOX ± bevacizumab)  
   – Rationale: Treat occult micrometastases, assess tumor biology, and potentially downsize liver lesions; high CEA (200 ng/mL) suggests aggressive disease.  

B. Restaging with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI and volumetric liver analysis after chemotherapy  
   – Rationale: Confirm continued resectability, calculate FLR, and detect any new extra‑hepatic sites.  

C. Surgical phase (choice based on FLR assessment)  
   • If FLR ≥30 % in a normal liver, proceed with simultaneous resection of the sigmoid primary (segmental colectomy with oncologic margins) and liver metastases (anatomic or non‑anatomic resections preserving segments I, IV, and sufficient parenchyma).  
   • If FLR is insufficient, adopt a staged approach: first, portal vein embolization (PVE) of the lobe to be resected, followed by delayed liver resection; the colon primary can be resected either before or after liver surgery depending on operative risk.  

D. Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 12 cycles (including neoadjuvant courses)  
   – Rationale: Consolidate systemic control and reduce recurrence risk in a high‑risk patient (CEA > 100 ng/mL, N1 disease).  

E. Surveillance protocol (CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging every 6 months for the first 2 years)  
   – Rationale: Early detection of recurrence for timely intervention.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Liver disease is limited to two lesions (3 cm in segment II, 4 cm in segment IVa) with preservation of the middle hepatic vein, indicating that an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection can achieve R0 while preserving adequate future liver remnant.  
  • No other extra‑hepatic sites are reported, and the primary tumor, although T4N2, is technically resectable with a right hemicolectomy (potentially extended to adjacent structures).  
  • High‑risk oncologic features (T4, N2, KRAS mutation, elevated CEA) warrant systemic therapy first to improve the chance of long‑term disease control, but they do not preclude resection.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
   – Rationale: Down‑stage microscopic disease, treat high‑risk biology, assess tumor response, and potentially convert borderline lesions to unequivocal resectability.  

B. Restaging with contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen and liver MRI after chemotherapy.  
   – Rationale: Confirm that liver lesions remain resectable, evaluate for new extra‑hepatic disease, and calculate future liver remnant volume.  

C. Surgical resection of the primary colon tumor (right hemicolectomy with en‑bloc resection of involved adjacent structures if necessary).  
   – Rationale: Primary tumor control prevents obstruction/bleeding; performing it after systemic therapy allows assessment of disease stability and reduces peri‑operative morbidity compared with simultaneous major liver resection.  

D. Liver‑directed surgery (segmental resection of segment II and segment IVa, preserving the middle hepatic vein).  
   – Rationale: Achieve R0 margins on both metastases while maintaining sufficient functional liver parenchyma; timing after primary resection allows recovery and completion of planned chemotherapy course.  

E. Completion of adjuvant systemic therapy to reach a total of 6 months (or longer per protocol) and consideration of maintenance therapy.  
   – Rationale: Consolidate response, address micrometastatic disease, and improve disease‑free survival; KRAS mutation excludes EGFR‑targeted agents.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases located in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. MRI confirms preservation of the middle hepatic vein and no major vascular invasion. Both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections (in case of effective tumor shrinkage with neoadjuvant therapy) or left hepatectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and favorable anatomical location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: control of the primary tumor
• The elevated CEA level (95 ng/mL) and right-sided T4N2 colon cancer represents locally advanced disease and is the immediate oncologic priority.
• Given the high CEA level (95 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Assess potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel, duodenum)
• 3 options
-	Perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis, first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications.
-	Perform an derivation ileostomy first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications during chemotherapy.
-	Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period allows treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Liver surgery after restaging
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan restaging.
• If tumor response is observed on primary cancer : proceed to oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis
• If tumor response is observed on liver metastases, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment II wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment IVa wedge/segmentectomy.
• If stability or progression is observed, proceed to anatomic left hepatectomy preserving the middle hepatic vein guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Man, 47 years old,at the abdominal CT scan T3N0 upper rectal cancer with three liver metastases (segments VI, VII and VIII), sizes 1-2 cm. CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. No other lesions on PET.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases primarily resectable, considered for combined treatment after short-course pelvic radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable).  
- Rationale:  
  • Three hepatic lesions, each 1‑2 cm, located in segments VI, VII and VIII – all within the right posterior sector, allowing a non‑anatomical or limited anatomical resection with preservation of >30 % functional liver remnant in a normal liver.  
  • No reported vascular invasion (portal/hepatic veins) or biliary involvement.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on PET.  
  • Primary rectal tumor is T3N0, without distant nodal disease, making it amenable to curative‑intent treatment.  
  • The need to confirm adequate future liver remnant (FLR) volume and liver function (Child‑Pugh, ICG) keeps the case in the “potentially resectable” category pending those data.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy)  
   – Provides rapid down‑staging of the upper rectal primary, facilitates subsequent surgery, and aligns with the MDT plan for combined treatment.  

B. Systemic peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS wild‑type)  
   – Treats micrometastatic disease, may further shrink liver lesions, and serves as a test of tumor biology; response will guide timing of liver resection.  

C. Re‑assessment imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) after chemotherapy  
   – Verify that FLR remains adequate, confirm no new lesions, and assess response of hepatic metastases.  

D. Liver‑directed surgery (either staged or simultaneous depending on intra‑operative assessment)  
   – Perform limited non‑anatomical resections or a segmentectomy of segments VI‑VIII, preserving sufficient FLR; consider portal vein embolization only if FLR is borderline.  

E. Rectal surgery (total mesorectal excision)  
   – Schedule after liver resection once the patient has recovered from chemotherapy; alternatively, a simultaneous colorectal and liver resection can be considered in a high‑volume center if operative risk is acceptable.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy (additional 3‑6 cycles)  
   – Completes a full peri‑operative regimen to reduce recurrence risk, especially given elevated pre‑operative CEA.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three small liver metastases (1–2 cm) located in segments VI, VII, and VIII, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Although confined to the right liver, the lesions seem technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution pelvic MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm primary tumor location, circumferential and distal margins, lymph nodes involvement, invasion of fascia recti. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and pelvic MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both primary tumor and liver metastases

  • No radiologic evidence of major vascular (portal/hepatic vein) invasion or biliary obstruction.  
  • Expected future liver remnant >70 % (well above the 20‑30 % safety threshold for a normal liver).  
  • Primary colon tumor is T3N0 and surgically accessible (right hemicolectomy).  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease on the available CT scan.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (2–3 months)  
   - Regimen: FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR (cetuximab) given BRAF wild‑type and presumed KRAS wild‑type; consider bevacizumab if contraindications to anti‑EGFR.  
   - Rationale: Treat occult micrometastases, assess tumor biology, and potentially increase resectability confidence.  

B. Restaging imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI or triphasic CT) after neoadjuvant therapy  
   - Rationale: Confirm that lesions remain resectable, evaluate response, and rule out new extra‑hepatic sites.  

C. Simultaneous surgical resection (single operative session)  
   - Procedure: Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy + liver‑directed surgery (segmentectomy of III and VI or wedge resections with ≥1 cm margins).  
   - Rationale: Limited hepatic disease, low operative morbidity with combined approach, avoids two separate recoveries, and shortens overall treatment time.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of 6 months total chemotherapy)  
   - Continue the same regimen used neoadjuvantly, adjusting for postoperative tolerance.  
   - Rationale: Improves disease‑free survival in resected colorectal liver metastases.

• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first wedge resection of segment III and a wedge resection of segment VI aiming while preserving maximal liver parenchyma, for ≥1 mm R0 margin and a right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2-D3 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes).

• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles).

Case_Content:
Man, 49 years old, T2N0 rectal tumor associated with a single 2.8 cm liver metastasis in segment V at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Single metastasis, resectable upfront, surgery considered after local treatment of the primary.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline between upfront resectable and requiring neoadjuvant therapy).  
- Justification:  
  • Single liver lesion, 2.8 cm, located in segment V – amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with preservation of adequate future liver remnant (FLR > 30 % in a normal liver).  
  • No radiologic evidence of additional hepatic or extra‑hepatic disease on the provided CT.  
  • Primary rectal cancer is T2N0, indicating limited depth of invasion and no nodal involvement, but rectal location typically warrants neoadjuvant treatment to reduce local recurrence risk.  
  • KRAS mutation does not affect surgical resectability but may influence systemic therapy choice.  
  • Therefore, while the hepatic disease is technically resectable, the overall treatment plan must incorporate neoadjuvant therapy for the rectal primary, making the case “potentially resectable” pending completion of that step.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) for the rectal primary  
   - Rationale: T2N0 rectal tumors, especially those located in the mid‑ or low‑rectum, benefit from pre‑operative CRT to improve local control and down‑stage the tumor, facilitating sphincter‑preserving surgery.  

B. Systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) concurrent with or following CRT  
   - Rationale: KRAS‑mutated disease warrants an oxaliplatin‑based doublet; systemic therapy also addresses micrometastatic disease and may further shrink the liver lesion, increasing the safety margin for hepatic resection.  

C. Surgical resection of the rectal primary (total mesorectal excision – TME)  
   - Timing: Performed 6–8 weeks after completion of CRT, once tumor response is confirmed on MRI.  
   - Rationale: Definitive local control of the primary; allows assessment of resection margins before proceeding to liver surgery.  

D. Hepatic resection of the segment V metastasis  
   - Timing: 4–6 weeks after rectal surgery, provided the patient has recovered and liver function is adequate.  
   - Technique: Segment V wedge or anatomical resection with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance to ensure negative margins (R0) while preserving FLR.  
   - Rationale: Isolated, small lesion permits curative‑intent resection; staged approach reduces operative stress and allows optimal postoperative monitoring.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy (if indicated by pathology)  
   - Rationale: Depending on final pathology (e.g., lymphovascular invasion, margin status), additional cycles of oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy may be offered to reduce recurrence risk.

• Consider image-guided ablation of the single lesion <3cm using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,

• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• This combined approach avoids multiple surgeries and is safe for a solitary peripheral metastasis.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven bilobar liver metastases, sizes 1 to 4 cm at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: vascular contact with the right portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Metastases not resectable upfront, considered for conversion chemotherapy FOLFOX + bevacizumab.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable after down‑staging.  
- Justification:  
  • Seven bilobar metastases (1–4 cm) exceed the usual criteria for upfront resection (limited number, unilobar disease, adequate future liver remnant).  
  • Vascular contact with the right portal branch indicates possible need for portal vein embolization or complex parenchymal‑sparing techniques.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease reported, and the primary tumor is still potentially resectable, satisfying the oncologic principle of R0 resection of all disease.  
  • Current systemic therapy (FOLFOX + bevacizumab) is the standard conversion regimen for KRAS‑mutated, high‑CEA colorectal liver metastases, offering a realistic chance of sufficient tumor shrinkage to achieve resectability.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Conversion systemic therapy – Initiate FOLFOX + bevacizumab for 3–6 months.  
   - Rationale: Aim to reduce tumor burden, improve resectability, and assess tumor biology (CEA trend, radiologic response).  

B. Restaging and functional assessment – Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted imaging) and triple‑phase CT; obtain volumetric analysis of future liver remnant (FLR) and assess portal venous flow.  
   - Rationale: Determine degree of response, quantify FLR; if FLR <30 % (or <40 % in steatotic liver) plan hypertrophy.  

C. Hypertrophy induction (if needed) – Perform right portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if FLR insufficient after chemotherapy.  
   - Rationale: Secure adequate postoperative liver volume to reduce risk of post‑hepatectomy liver failure.  

D. Surgical resection –  
   1. Primary colon tumor: If not yet resected and patient’s condition permits, perform simultaneous colectomy with liver resection (if limited hepatic disease after down‑staging) or staged colectomy after hepatic surgery.  
   2. Hepatic metastases: Pursue parenchymal‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resections to achieve R0 margins; consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (right hepatectomy first, followed by left‑lateral resection) if disease distribution remains bilobar despite response.  
   - Rationale: Achieve complete (R0) removal of all visible disease while preserving sufficient liver parenchyma.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy – Resume or continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 3–6 months post‑resection, with consideration of anti‑EGFR agents if future molecular profiling permits.  
   - Rationale: Reduce risk of recurrence given initial high tumor burden and KRAS mutation.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven bilobar liver metastases (1–4 cm) associated with vascular contact with the right portal branch and no reported extrahepatic disease. The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and portal contact make a complete R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant unlikely with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (520 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX + bevacizumab.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is tumor downsizing, separation from portal structures, and reduction in the number/volume of lesions to achieve secondary resectability.

C. Early and repeated radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response, particularly the relationship of lesions to the right portal branch and overall liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA dynamics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Consider surgery if chemotherapy induces:
– Reduction in lesion size and number allowing parenchymal-sparing resections or staged hepatectomy or combined resection and ablation.
– Clearance from portal structures.
– Feasibility of achieving R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern and tumor location.
• Portal vein embolization may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If no adequate response
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T3N1M1 sigmoid tumor, four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) with one in contact with the right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 240 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar involvement for conversion, imaging to be re-evaluated after 4 cycles of chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Four bilobar metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) indicate disease that can be cleared surgically but requires careful planning of future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • One lesion abuts the right hepatic vein, raising concern for vascular involvement but not yet overt invasion; this may be amenable to parenchymal‑sparing resection or vascular reconstruction after down‑staging.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; absence of contraindicating comorbidities is assumed but not confirmed.  
  • RAS wild‑type status predicts good response to modern conversion chemotherapy, supporting the possibility of achieving resectability.  
  • Current imaging does not demonstrate sufficient FLR after a single‑stage major hepatectomy; thus conversion therapy and/or staged approach are indicated before definitive surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Conversion systemic therapy – Initiate 4 cycles of a doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status. Goal: tumor shrinkage to facilitate parenchymal‑sparing resection and improve FLR.  
B. Restaging and volumetric assessment – After chemotherapy, repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT volumetry. Evaluate:  
   • Response of each lesion (size reduction, disappearance).  
   • Relationship of the right‑vein‑adjacent lesion to vascular structures.  
   • Calculated FLR; aim for ≥30 % in a normal liver or ≥40 % if prior chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected.  
C. Surgical planning based on restaging  
   • If FLR is adequate and all lesions become resectable with parenchymal‑sparing techniques, proceed to simultaneous colorectal resection and staged or single‑stage liver resection (preferably parenchymal‑sparing, e.g., segmental/sectional resections).  
   • If FLR remains insufficient, plan a two‑stage hepatectomy:  
        – Stage 1: Resection of left‑lateral lesions (segments II‑III) combined with primary tumor resection; portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left liver.  
        – Interval imaging (4–6 weeks) to confirm FLR hypertrophy.  
        – Stage 2: Right‑sided hepatectomy (segments VI‑VIII) with careful management of the right hepatic vein lesion (possible wedge resection with vein reconstruction or en‑bloc resection if still involved).  
   • Throughout, maintain oncologic margins ≥1 cm (or R0) and preserve vascular inflow/outflow.  
D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy and surveillance – Post‑operative systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of oxaliplatin‑based regimen ± anti‑EGFR) for 3–6 months, followed by regular CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI every 3–6 months) for at least 2 years.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, and VIII), one of which is in contact with the right hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. The bilobar distribution and venous contact make a complete R0 parenchymal-sparing resection unlikely with an upfront approach while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely resectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all 4 lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (240 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI or FOLFIRINOX) combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status.
• The objective is tumor downsizing, separation from the right hepatic vein, and reduction of bilobar tumor burden to enable secondary resectability.

C. Early radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after 4 cycles as planned to reassess:
– Relationship of the segment VIII lesion to the right hepatic vein.
– Global tumor response and potential for parenchymal-sparing resections.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered if imaging shows:
– Clearance from the right hepatic vein.
– Feasibility of multiple parenchymal-sparing resections or a staged hepatectomy.
– Adequate future liver remnant after planned resections.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Combined parenchymal-sparing resections of segments II, III, VI, and VIII.
• If necessary, a two-stage hepatectomy strategy depending on response pattern and FLR considerations.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥8 lesions), maximum size 4.5 cm, partial contact with the IVC at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 890 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, potentially resectable after major response to FOLFOXIRI.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (conversion case).  
- Justification:  
  • ≥8 hepatic lesions, some likely bilobar, exceed typical criteria for upfront resection.  
  • Largest lesion 4.5 cm and partial contact with the inferior vena cava raise concerns for vascular involvement and margin clearance.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease beyond the colon primary, but the extent of liver involvement suggests that an R0 resection cannot be achieved with the current tumor burden and without compromising future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • Current systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI) has the potential to down‑size lesions and possibly convert to resectable status, which aligns with contemporary conversion‑therapy algorithms.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Continue/optimise FOLFOXIRI (consider adding bevacizumab or anti‑EGFR agent given KRAS/NRAS wild‑type and BRAF wild‑type).  
   - Goal: achieve ≥30 % reduction in total tumor volume and assess radiologic response.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment (after 8–12 weeks of chemotherapy)  
   - Multiphasic contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with liver volumetry.  
   - Evaluate FLR; aim for ≥30 % of total liver volume (≥40 % if underlying liver disease).  
   - Assess IVC involvement: determine if tumor abuts <180° of the circumference and whether vascular reconstruction would be required.  
   - Consider PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Conversion surgical planning  
   - If sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR, plan a two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS depending on lesion distribution and FLR deficit.  
   - If FLR remains marginal, perform portal vein embolisation (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
   - For IVC contact, evaluate need for limited IVC resection with patch angioplasty or graft; involve vascular surgery early.  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - If the primary has not been resected, schedule a coordinated resection either:  
     • Simultaneous colon and liver resection (if patient fitness allows and liver surgery is limited), or  
     • Staged approach with colon resection first, followed by liver surgery after recovery and systemic therapy response.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Post‑operative continuation of systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 3–6 months, tailored to pathologic response and margin status.  
   - Consider enrollment in clinical trials for high‑risk conversion patients.  

F. Surveillance  
   - Serial CEA, imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable upfront, with a possibility of secondary resectability only after major tumor response.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:

– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Preoperative portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy is needed.

• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, goal of volumetric reduction with chemotherapy.
Response:

Potentially resectable. The patient has bilobar disease (six lesions 2‑5 cm) with involvement of the middle hepatic vein, which currently precludes a single‑stage anatomic resection with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR). A. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the upper rectal primary (long‑course 5‑FU‑based RT).  
   – Rationale: T3N2 rectal cancer benefits from down‑staging to improve sphincter preservation and local control before systemic therapy.

   – Rationale: Ensures definitive control of the primary tumor after systemic disease has been addressed.

G. Adjuvant systemic therapy (optional) based on final pathology, margin status, and postoperative recovery.  
   – Rationale: To eradicate residual microscopic disease and reduce recurrence risk.

Case_Content:
Man, 67 years old, T3N1M1 right colon tumor, five liver metastases (segments IV, V, VII, VIII), sizes 1.5-3.8 cm at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 270 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Potentially resectable after partial response to systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Five hepatic lesions confined to segments IV, V, VII, and VIII, each ≤ 3.8 cm, without reported extra‑hepatic disease.  
  • Partial radiologic response to systemic therapy suggests tumor shrinkage and possible conversion to resectable status.  
  • RAS wild‑type status predicts better response to chemotherapy and suitability for anti‑EGFR agents if needed.  
  • No contraindicating factors such as major biliary obstruction, severe hepatic dysfunction, or uncontrolled extra‑hepatic metastases have been described.  
  • Resectability hinges on achieving an R0 margin while preserving an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is present).  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continue systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX + anti‑EGFR if not already used) for an additional 2–3 months to maximize tumor response and allow for optimal down‑staging.

Woman, 71 years old, T4N1M1 transverse colon cancer, nine bilobar liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 950 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: several lesions close to the hepatic veins.
MDT Discussion: Liver involvement not resectable upfront, conversion strategy considered.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: potentially resectable (borderline) after down‑staging.  
- Justification:  
  • Nine bilobar hepatic metastases exceed the typical criteria for upfront resection (generally ≤4 lesions or ≤5 cm total tumor burden).  
  • Lesions are close to major hepatic veins, raising concern for insufficient negative margins and risk of vascular injury.  
  • High CEA (950 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation are adverse biological factors that predict lower response to anti‑EGFR therapy and higher recurrence risk, but do not preclude resection if adequate tumor shrinkage is achieved.  
  • Primary tumor is T4N1, indicating aggressive disease; however, the absence of documented extra‑hepatic disease beyond the liver keeps the patient in the realm of conversion‑potential.  
  • Current imaging shows no extra‑hepatic metastases; therefore, with effective systemic therapy and possible liver‑directed interventions, a curative intent resection could become feasible.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (2–3 months)  
   - Regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
   - Rationale: Maximizes tumor response, addresses micrometastatic disease, and may convert borderline lesions to resectable status.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment (after induction)  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and volumetric CT to evaluate tumor shrinkage, lesion‑to‑vein distance, and future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
   - Assess liver function (bilirubin, albumin, ICG clearance) and performance status.  
   - Rationale: Determines whether sufficient down‑staging and FLR (>30 % in normal liver) have been achieved for safe resection.  

C. Adjunctive liver‑directed measures (if needed)  
   - If FLR remains marginal, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to hypertrophy the remnant.  
   - If residual lesions abut hepatic veins, evaluate selective hepatic vein embolization or intra‑arterial Y‑90 radioembolization to enhance necrosis.  
   - Rationale: Increases resectability by expanding functional liver reserve and improving margin clearance.  

D. Surgical resection (once criteria met)  
   - Primary colon tumor: perform oncologic colectomy (segmental resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) either simultaneously with liver surgery if patient’s physiologic reserve permits, or as a staged procedure prior to hepatic resection.  
   - Liver: execute a curative‑intent hepatectomy (potentially two‑stage or ALPPS) aiming for R0 margins; preserve ≥30 % FLR, protect major hepatic veins, and consider intra‑operative ultrasound for lesion localization.  
   - Rationale: Achieves complete macroscopic clearance of both primary and metastatic disease, offering the best chance for long‑term survival.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., fluoropyrimidine‑based) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, tailored to response and tolerance.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   - Rationale: Reduces risk of recurrence and enables early detection of new disease.

  • The MDT already considered a two‑stage hepatectomy, indicating that with down‑staging and hypertrophy strategies the FLR could become adequate.  
  • Therefore, the disease is not outright unresectable but requires conversion/down‑staging and careful volumetric planning, placing it in the “potentially resectable” category.

A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   – Initiate an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.

   – Resume systemic therapy (e.g., maintenance fluoropyrimidine ± anti‑VEGF) after surgical recovery, guided by pathology (margin status, response) and postoperative CEA trend.  
   – Rationale: addresses microscopic residual disease and reduces recurrence risk.

- Classification: Potentially resectable.

  • RAS wild‑type status supports a favorable biology and eligibility for targeted systemic therapy.  
  • The MDT notes “feasible in a single surgery,” indicating that an R0 resection could be achieved with a parenchymal‑sparing approach, but the assessment lacks quantitative data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume and hepatic functional reserve; therefore the case is deemed potentially rather than definitively resectable pending those evaluations.

A. Comprehensive pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis (or PET‑CT) to reconfirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease.

   – Initiate 3‑4 months of doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR agent (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type disease, aiming to:  
     • Reduce tumor burden and increase the likelihood of an R0 resection,  
     • Treat occult micrometastatic disease,  
     • Provide a biologic test of tumor responsiveness.

   – Repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) and repeat volumetry.  
   – If lesions have responded or remained stable and FLR is adequate, proceed to surgery.

   – If intra‑operative findings reveal unresectable disease (vascular invasion, insufficient margin), abort resection and consider conversion therapies.

   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 4‑6 cycles of FOLFOX) after adequate recovery, per current NCCN/ESMO guidelines for resected colorectal liver metastases.
