• Given the high CEA level (240 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA level (240 ng/mL) and relatively early recurrence (2 years), a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability is confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing wedge/segmental resections or ablation of segments II and VIII guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Five residual hepatic lesions are well‑defined after a 60 % volumetric response, indicating a favorable tumor biology and chemosensitivity.  
  • CEA decline from 880 to 180 ng/mL supports biochemical response.  
  • Bilobar distribution remains, which traditionally limits immediate one‑stage resection unless an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • No information is provided regarding lesion size, proximity to major hepatic vessels/ducts, or FLR volume; therefore, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed, but conversion to resectability is plausible with appropriate adjuncts (e.g., portal vein embolization, two‑stage or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS).  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging (within 2–3 weeks).  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to define lesion size, segmental location, vascular involvement, and to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Obtain liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy, and calculate FLR volume using volumetric software.  

B. Multidisciplinary decision on surgical approach (after restaging).  
   - If FLR ≥30 % in a normal liver (or ≥40 % in a chemotherapy‑injured liver) and lesions are amenable to R0 resection, plan a single‑stage combined colorectal and hepatic resection (simultaneous) or a staged approach (colon first, then liver) based on patient performance status and operative risk.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS to hypertrophy the future remnant, followed by delayed hepatic resection.  

C. Surgical execution.  
   - Perform oncologic resection of the primary left‑sided colon cancer with adequate lymphadenectomy (aim for ≥12 nodes).  
   - Conduct parenchymal‑sparing hepatic resections (segmentectomy/partial hepatectomy) to achieve negative margins while preserving maximal functional liver tissue.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and guide resection.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy.  
   - Resume or modify systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, considering the prior bevacizumab exposure and any molecular markers (RAS/RAF status).  
   - Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for surveillance.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab, the patient shows a major radiologic and biologic response (≈60% volumetric reduction; CEA from 880 to 180 ng/mL). MRI now demonstrates five well-defined residual liver lesions without reported extrahepatic disease. In this context of marked downsizing and clearer lesion delineation, a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant appears potentially achievable. This pattern is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Immediate high-quality restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to reassess precise segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships after tumor shrinkage.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical conversion strategy
• If imaging confirms feasibility, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of all five lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may be performed as a single-stage or staged hepatectomy.
• The goal is complete clearance of residual disease while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic chemotherapy after recovery to complete a total of approximately 6 months of treatment (including preoperative cycles).

E. Surveillance
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially very high tumor burden.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Current status: potentially resectable (not immediately resectable).  
- Rationale:  
  • Eight metastases distributed bilaterally indicate that a single‑stage R0 resection would require an extensive hepatectomy with an inadequate future liver remnant (FLR < 30 % in most scenarios).  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic CT, which is favorable, but the number and bilobar location exceed typical criteria for upfront resection.  
  • Radiologic disease is stable after 4 months of FOLFIRI, suggesting tumor biology is not rapidly progressive, allowing a chance for down‑staging with additional systemic or liver‑directed therapy.  
  • Liver function (bilirubin, albumin, ICG clearance) and performance status are not provided; assuming they are acceptable, conversion to resectability remains feasible.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continue systemic therapy with a conversion‑focused regimen  
   - Switch to FOLFOX ± bevacizumab (or add anti‑EGFR therapy if RAS/BRAF wild‑type) for 2–3 months to attempt tumor shrinkage and improve resectability.  
   - Rationale: FOLFOX‑based regimens have higher response rates in colorectal liver metastases; bevacizumab can enhance tumor necrosis and facilitate subsequent surgery.  

B. Re‑assessment imaging and functional evaluation  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) and volumetry after the additional systemic cycle; repeat CEA measurement.  
   - Assess FLR volume; if FLR < 30 % but expected to increase, consider portal vein embolization (PVE).  
   - Rationale: Objective response and adequate FLR are prerequisites for safe hepatic resection.  

C. Consider liver‑directed conversion techniques if needed  
   - If response is limited but lesions become amenable to a staged approach, options include:  
     • Two‑stage hepatectomy with PVE between stages.  
     • Associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) in selected patients.  
     • Hepatic arterial infusion (HAI) chemotherapy or radioembolization (Y‑90) for bulky lesions.  
   - Rationale: These modalities can down‑size lesions or induce hypertrophy of the future liver remnant, converting an unresectable burden to resectable.  

D. Surgical resection  
   - If post‑conversion imaging shows ≤4 lesions confined to one or two segments with an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in steatotic liver), proceed to an anatomic or non‑anatomic hepatic resection aiming for R0 margins.  
   - Simultaneous or staged resection of the primary sigmoid tumor should be planned based on oncologic urgency and patient fitness (e.g., sigmoid resection first if symptomatic, otherwise combined resection after liver clearance).  
   - Rationale: Achieving an R0 liver resection after systemic down‑staging offers the best chance for long‑term survival.  

E. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) for 3–6 months post‑resection, tailored to molecular profile and prior tolerance.  
   - Rationale: Reduces risk of recurrence after curative‑intent surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases and, after 4 months of FOLFIRI, shows radiological stability with persistently elevated CEA (420 ng/mL). The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and absence of meaningful tumor downsizing make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Continuation and adaptation of systemic therapy
• Given the absence of radiologic response and stable high CEA, modification of the systemic regimen should be considered according to MDT discussion.
• The objective remains to achieve tumor downsizing sufficient to allow potential secondary resectability.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to detect any delayed response or change in lesion distribution.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant reduction in lesion size and number occurs, enabling parenchymal-sparing resections or multiples ablations or staged hepatectomy with adequate future liver remnant.

D. Alternative local strategies
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Initial burden of ten hepatic lesions suggests a high tumor load, but systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI) has produced a partial response with disappearance of three lesions and ≥40 % shrinkage of the remaining lesions, indicating chemosensitivity.  
  • MRI shows conversion of several lesions to hypo‑intense (likely necrotic) tissue, supporting a favorable biological response.  
  • The patient is 49 years old, presumably with preserved performance status, which favors aggressive local therapy.  
  • Resectability hinges on the ability to achieve R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is present). Without precise data on lesion distribution (unilobar vs bilobar), proximity to major vascular/biliary structures, and volumetric assessment, a definitive “resectable” label cannot be assigned; therefore the case is deemed potentially resectable pending further evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Obtain high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with liver volumetry, and a PET‑CT to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Perform liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and calculate indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy to quantify functional FLR.  
   - Rationale: Precise mapping of residual disease and functional reserve is essential to determine feasibility of curative hepatectomy and to plan potential portal vein embolization (PVE) or staged resection.

B. Multidisciplinary decision on conversion strategy  
   - If imaging confirms residual disease confined to one lobe or amenable to limited bilateral resections with adequate FLR, proceed to surgical planning.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, schedule PVE (or LVD) to hypertrophy the future remnant; consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS if disease is bilobar but limited.  
   - Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI or switch to a regimen incorporating targeted agents based on molecular profile) for 2–3 additional cycles to maximize tumor shrinkage and address micrometastatic disease.  
   - Rationale: Optimizing tumor response and FLR volume maximizes the chance of an R0 resection while minimizing postoperative liver failure.

C. Surgical intervention  
   - Perform curative‑intent liver resection (anatomic or non‑anatomic) aiming for negative margins (R0).  
   - If the primary rectal tumor remains unresected, coordinate simultaneous or staged colorectal resection (e.g., low anterior resection) depending on oncologic urgency and patient condition.  
   - Rationale: Achieving complete removal of hepatic disease offers the only chance for long‑term survival in colorectal liver metastases; simultaneous resection may reduce overall treatment time if feasible.

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively (typically 3–6 months) tailored to molecular profile (e.g., anti‑EGFR or anti‑VEGF agents if indicated).  
   - Implement a surveillance schedule with CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first two years.  
   - Rationale: Adjuvant therapy reduces recurrence risk; close surveillance enables early detection of new metastases.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Unresectable at present.  
- Rationale:  
  • Only two hepatic lesions (segments VII and VIII) would be technically resectable with a right hepatectomy, but resectability also requires favorable tumor biology.  
  • The lesions have progressed after 8 cycles of FOLFOX, indicating chemoresistance and aggressive disease.  
  • Rising CEA (950 ng/mL) supports biologically aggressive disease.  
  • Current MDT consensus states “no surgical window,” reflecting that the disease is not presently amenable to curative resection.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Second‑line systemic therapy – initiate FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab (or enrol in a clinical trial).  
   – Rationale: aim to achieve disease control or down‑staging when first‑line FOLFOX failed.  

B. Re‑evaluation after 2–3 months – repeat contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI, assess CEA trend, and evaluate performance status.  
   – Rationale: determine whether the tumor has stabilized, responded, or further progressed.  

C. Conversion to resectability (if imaging shows response or stable disease) – plan right hepatectomy (or parenchymal‑sparing resection) ensuring ≥30 % future liver remnant and negative margins.  
   – Rationale: conversion surgery is feasible only after achieving at least disease stability; adequate FLR must be confirmed.  

D. Palliative/locoregional options (if disease continues to progress) – consider Y‑90 radio‑embolization, percutaneous ablation, or best‑supportive care.  
   – Rationale: provides symptom control and may modestly prolong survival when curative intent is no longer possible.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient shows progression of liver disease under FOLFOX with enlargement of two lesions in segments VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) and markedly elevated CEA (950 ng/mL). This radiologic progression under systemic therapy indicates biologically aggressive disease and makes a complete R0 resection with adequate oncologic control not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given progression on FOLFOX, a change of systemic regimen is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab: complete disappearance of four foci and reduction of others at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA normalized.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response in several segments, uncertainty regarding microscopic persistence.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Seven hepatic metastases initially, but after 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab four lesions are radiologically absent and the remaining lesions have decreased in size, indicating good tumor response.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; CEA normalization supports systemic disease control.  
  • Resectability hinges on ability to achieve an R0 resection with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR). Because the exact distribution and residual tumor burden are not detailed, the case cannot be declared outright resectable, but the response makes a curative‑intent liver operation feasible pending further anatomic assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging imaging – Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (gadoxetate) and a PET‑CT.  
   • Purpose: confirm the true extent of residual disease, detect any occult extra‑hepatic sites, and allow precise volumetric calculation of the FLR.  

B. Multidisciplinary re‑evaluation – Review imaging, liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance), and performance status.  
   • If lesions are confined to one lobe or can be cleared with a single‑stage resection leaving an FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in steatotic or chemotherapy‑injured liver), proceed to curative surgery.  
   • If disease is bilobar with insufficient FLR, consider a staged approach (e.g., portal vein embolization to hypertrophy the future remnant, two‑stage hepatectomy, or ALPPS) based on lesion location.  

C. Surgical resection – Perform liver‑directed surgery with intra‑operative ultrasound to locate any residual foci.  
   • Aim for R0 margins; use parenchymal‑sparing techniques when possible to preserve liver volume.  
   • If complete radiologic response is confirmed in some segments, those areas may be resected or left in situ after intra‑operative confirmation of negative margins.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy and surveillance – Resume systemic therapy (continue anti‑EGFR if still indicated, or switch to a fluoropyrimidine‑based regimen) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, followed by serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first two years.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab, four lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions have significantly decreased in size, with normalization of CEA. Despite this excellent response, the initial tumor burden and the phenomenon of “disappearing metastases” mean that viable microscopic disease may persist at the original sites. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but requires meticulous mapping of all initial metastatic locations before surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and systematically compare with pre-treatment imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy addressing initial disease map
• Plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided surgical approach that includes resection or ablation of all initial metastatic locations, not only residual visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to identify occult residual disease.
• Depending on lesion distribution, this may require a staged approach.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete surgical clearance of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • After 4 cycles of systemic therapy the number of hepatic lesions has decreased from ten to three, each <2 cm, indicating a major radiologic response.  
  • Marked tumor marker decline (CEA 1100 → 80 ng/mL) supports biologic response.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported in the summary.  
  • Current hepatobiliary criteria consider ≤4 lesions ≤3 cm, confined to one or two hepatic sectors, with an anticipated future liver remnant (FLR) ≥30 % in a normal liver, as potentially resectable.  
  • Definitive classification requires confirmation of lesion distribution, FLR volume, underlying liver function, and performance status; these data are not provided, hence the “potentially” qualifier.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and volumetric assessment  
   – Obtain high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with 3‑D volumetry, chest CT, and pelvic MRI to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease and to calculate FLR.  
   – Rationale: Precise mapping of lesion location and FLR is essential before committing to hepatic resection.  

B. Management of the primary rectal tumor  
   – If the primary remains locally advanced, proceed with neoadjuvant chemoradiation (long‑course 5‑FU based) or short‑course radiotherapy followed by delayed surgery, depending on T‑stage and mesorectal involvement.  
   – Rationale: Achieving local control of the rectal primary reduces risk of synchronous recurrence and aligns with curative intent.  

C. Liver‑directed intervention  
   – If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan a single‑stage parenchymal‑sparing resection (segmentectomy or wedge resection) of the three residual lesions, aiming for ≥1 cm negative margins.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to hypertrophy the future remnant, followed by resection after 4–6 weeks.  
   – Rationale: Parenchymal‑sparing approaches preserve hepatic reserve and reduce postoperative morbidity while maintaining oncologic adequacy.  

D. Post‑operative systemic therapy and surveillance  
   – Resume or intensify systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI or FOLFIRI + anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS wild‑type) for 3–6 months post‑resection.  
   – Implement surveillance with CEA, cross‑sectional imaging of chest/abdomen every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  
   – Rationale: Adjuvant therapy addresses microscopic disease and improves disease‑free survival; close surveillance enables early detection of recurrence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases, CEA 600 ng/mL. On FOLFOX: overall stability, two new lesions detected at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Limited progression on treatment, question of changing protocol.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Multiple bilobar hepatic metastases – current distribution likely exceeds safe future liver remnant without adjuncts (e.g., portal vein embolization).  
  • Presence of new extra‑hepatic lesions on thoraco‑abdominal CT (most commonly pulmonary) classifies disease as M1 with extra‑hepatic spread, which traditionally renders patients unresectable unless extra‑hepatic disease is limited and amenable to curative resection.  
  • Limited progression on FOLFOX suggests some chemosensitivity, indicating a possibility of down‑staging with intensified systemic therapy.  
  • No data on lesion size, number, vascular involvement, or functional liver reserve; therefore, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed at this time, but conversion to resectability remains plausible.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic therapy optimization (2–3 cycles)  
   – Switch to a more intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) or add targeted agents based on RAS/BRAF/MSI status.  
   – Rationale: Aim for maximal tumor shrinkage to achieve hepatic and extra‑hepatic disease control, increasing the chance of conversion to resectability.  

B. Restaging work‑up (after 8–12 weeks)  
   – Repeat high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver, chest CT, and PET‑CT if available.  
   – Assess response of hepatic lesions, size/number of extra‑hepatic lesions, and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
   – Rationale: Objective response will guide whether conversion surgery is feasible and whether extra‑hepatic disease remains resectable.  

C. Multidisciplinary decision point  
   – If hepatic disease down‑staged to ≤4 lesions confined to one lobe or amenable to two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS, proceed with hepatic resection.  
   – If extra‑hepatic disease is limited (e.g., ≤3 pulmonary nodules amenable to metastasectomy) and controlled, plan simultaneous or staged extra‑hepatic resection.  
   – Rationale: Curative intent surgery is justified only when all macroscopic disease can be removed with adequate liver function.  

D. Surgical execution (when criteria met)  
   – Perform portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if FLR <30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver.  
   – Conduct hepatic resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing) aiming for R0 margins.  
   – Address resectable pulmonary metastases either concurrently (if limited) or in a staged fashion within 4–6 weeks post‑hepatectomy.  
   – Rationale: Ensures oncologically adequate margins while preserving sufficient liver volume and minimizing postoperative morbidity.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   – Resume systemic therapy (potentially de‑escalated) for 3–6 months post‑resection, tailored to molecular profile.  
   – Consider enrollment in clinical trial if available.  
   – Rationale: Reduces risk of recurrence after major oncologic surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases with the appearance of two new lesions while on FOLFOX, indicating disease progression under systemic therapy. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and ongoing progression make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The appearance of new lesions under FOLFOX indicates resistance to the current regimen.
• A change of systemic protocol is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± targeted therapy depending on molecular profile).
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Residual disease consists of 7 hepatic lesions (6 stable, 1 progressing 5 cm in segment VII).  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic metastases.  
  • Absence of vascular invasion or biliary obstruction is not reported, but the number and bilateral distribution (implied by “ten initial lesions”) suggest that a curative‑intent resection could be achieved with a parenchymal‑sparing approach, two‑stage hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation, provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver) can be preserved.  
  • The progressing lesion is resectable in isolation (segment VII), and the three lesions that disappeared on imaging may represent complete radiologic response, reducing tumor burden.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging imaging  
   – Obtain liver‑specific MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences and a PET‑CT to precisely map the location, size, and vascular relationship of the six stable lesions and to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Rationale: Accurate anatomic mapping is essential to plan a parenchymal‑sparing resection or to decide on a two‑stage approach and to calculate FLR.  

B. Multidisciplinary systemic therapy optimization  
   – Continue or modify current chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) given KRAS mutation and prior partial response; consider adding a targeted agent (anti‑VEGF) if not already used.  
   – Rationale: Consolidate disease control, potentially down‑size the progressing segment VII lesion, and treat micrometastatic disease.  

C. Local control of the progressing lesion  
   – If the segment VII lesion remains resectable after restaging, plan a limited anatomical resection (segmentectomy) or a wedge resection combined with intra‑operative ultrasound.  
   – If resection would compromise FLR, consider percutaneous image‑guided ablation (RFA/MWA) or stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) as a bridge to surgery.  
   – Rationale: Eradication of the only progressing focus is required before a curative‑intent liver‑first strategy.  

D. Curative‑intent hepatic surgery  
   – Aim for a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy that removes all residual lesions while preserving ≥30 % FLR; if FLR is insufficient, employ portal vein embolization (PVE) followed by a second‑stage resection or consider ALPPS.  
   – Perform intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any additional occult lesions.  
   – Rationale: Achieving R0 resection with adequate liver reserve offers the best chance for long‑term survival.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 months) as adjuvant therapy.  
   – Schedule surveillance imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Initial disease was bilobar, meeting criteria for unresectable at presentation.  
  • After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI there is a radiologic complete response on thoraco‑abdominal CT and CEA is normalized, indicating excellent systemic control.  
  • Current imaging shows no visible hepatic lesions, but the absence of disease on CT does not guarantee eradication of microscopic disease; therefore surgical exploration with intra‑operative ultrasound (IOUS) is required to confirm true clearance and to assess the future liver remnant (FLR) should resection be needed.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging with high‑resolution liver MRI (gadoxetate‑enhanced) ± PET‑CT  
   - Rationale: MRI is more sensitive than CT for detecting residual hepatic disease; PET‑CT helps exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases that could alter the plan.  

B. Multidisciplinary review of restaging results  
   - Rationale: Confirm that no extra‑hepatic disease is present and that the FLR would be adequate (>30 % of total liver volume in a normal liver, >40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  

C. Surgical exploration with IOUS and targeted biopsies of prior metastatic sites  
   - If IOUS identifies residual lesions → perform anatomic or non‑anatomic liver resection (or wedge/segmental resection) to achieve R0 clearance.  
   - If IOUS is negative → obtain core biopsies from the previously involved segments to rule out microscopic disease.  

D. Decision based on intra‑operative pathology  
   - Negative biopsies and no macroscopic disease → forego major hepatectomy, close the abdomen, and proceed to surveillance.  
   - Positive biopsies or residual disease → complete appropriate hepatic resection with aim for negative margins while preserving adequate FLR.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of planned 12‑month total chemotherapy duration)  
   - Rationale: Consolidate response and treat potential micrometastatic disease; regimen may be continued FOLFOXIRI or switched to a maintenance protocol (e.g., fluoropyrimidine ± bevacizumab) based on tolerance and molecular profile.  

F. Post‑operative surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT of the liver every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually; consider PET‑CT if CEA rises.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer with bulky metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy: incomplete reduction, persistence of three lesions >5 cm. CEA 450 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Current classification: potentially resectable (borderline) – not immediately resectable.  
• Rationale: three hepatic lesions each >5 cm, persistent after 8 cycles of systemic therapy, indicating bulky disease that likely exceeds safe future liver remnant (FLR) limits and may involve major vascular structures. No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but the size and number place the case beyond conventional resectability criteria (≤5 cm, ≤4 lesions, adequate FLR ≥30 % in normal liver). Therefore, further down‑staging is required before a curative hepatectomy can be contemplated.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continue/optimise systemic therapy (2–3 additional cycles)  
   – Add biologic agent based on molecular profile (anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type, anti‑VEGF if RAS‑mutated).  
   – Goal: achieve greater tumor shrinkage to permit safe resection and improve CEA trend.  

B. Re‑evaluate hepatic disease after the additional cycles  
   – Multiphasic contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with volumetry.  
   – Assess FLR, lesion‑to‑vascular relationships, and response (RECIST).  

C. If sufficient down‑staging (lesions ≤5 cm, FLR ≥30 % or after portal vein embolisation) proceed to staged hepatic resection  
   – Consider two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS depending on lesion distribution and FLR deficit.  
   – Aim for R0 resection of all liver metastases.  

D. Address the primary colon tumor  
   – If liver resection can be performed safely with simultaneous right hemicolectomy, consider combined procedure.  
   – Otherwise, schedule curative colectomy 4–6 weeks after hepatic surgery once patient recovers, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy to complete peri‑operative systemic treatment.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bulky liver metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, there is only partial reduction with persistence of three large lesions >5 cm and persistently elevated CEA (450 ng/mL). The residual tumor burden and limited response make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The insufficient response to current chemotherapy requires modification of the systemic regimen or consider intra arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary cancer, according to MDT decision.
• The objective remains to achieve further tumor downsizing that may open a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Given the high CEA level (450 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, reducing lesion size and allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains insufficiently responsive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, operated two years earlier with a right hepatectomy for synchronous metastases from a left colon cancer. Surveillance: CEA 220 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, anatomically accessible, no extra-hepatic disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
  • Recurrence is confined to the left lateral segments (II and III) with no extra‑hepatic disease, satisfying anatomic criteria for resection.  
  • Prior right hepatectomy has already removed the right liver; the remaining liver consists mainly of segments II, III, and IV. Resection of both lesions would leave only segment IV, raising concern for insufficient future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • Absence of extra‑hepatic disease and KRAS mutation do not preclude surgery, but functional liver reserve and FLR volume are critical determinants. Hence the case is not outright resectable but may become resectable after optimization (e.g., portal vein embolization, neoadjuvant therapy, or ablative alternatives).

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and functional assessment  
   – Obtain triphasic CT or contrast‑enhanced MRI with volumetric analysis of the FLR.  
   – Perform liver function testing (Child‑Pugh, ICG clearance, MELD) and assess performance status.  
   – Rationale: Quantify residual liver volume and functional reserve to decide if immediate surgery is safe.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Initiate 2–3 months of FOLFOX (or FOLFIRI) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated disease (anti‑EGFR agents ineffective).  
   – Rationale: Control micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially downsize lesions to facilitate a parenchymal‑sparing approach.  

C. Re‑evaluation after systemic therapy  
   – Repeat imaging and volumetry; calculate FLR percentage (target >30 % in normal liver, >40 % after chemotherapy).  
   – Rationale: Determine whether the liver has hypertrophied sufficiently or if lesions have responded enough to permit limited resection or ablation.  

D. Local definitive treatment (choose based on findings in C)  
   1. If FLR adequate and lesions amenable:  
      – Perform parenchymal‑sparing left‑lateral resection (segment II/III wedge or segmentectomy) preserving segment IV, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound.  
   2. If FLR inadequate but lesions responsive:  
      – Conduct portal vein embolization of the left portal branches to hypertrophy segment IV, followed by staged resection after 4–6 weeks.  
   3. If FLR remains insufficient or lesions are borderline for resection:  
      – Proceed with percutaneous image‑guided ablation (RFA or microwave) of both lesions, possibly combined with intra‑operative ablation if needed.  
   – Rationale: Tailor the local approach to achieve complete oncologic clearance while preserving enough functional liver tissue.  

E. Post‑operative / post‑ablation management  
   – Resume systemic therapy (maintenance bevacizumab or appropriate regimen) based on pathology and response.  
   – Implement surveillance protocol: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT/MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases in segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm) occurring in the left lateral section after a prior right hepatectomy, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesions are peripherally located but arise in the only remaining functional liver. Resection is technically feasible but must strictly preserve adequate parenchyma and inflow/outflow. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of previous major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered resectable with a strict parenchymal-sparing strategy, pending volumetric confirmation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative volumetric and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and ensure preservation of sufficient functional parenchyma.
• Assess portal inflow and venous outflow carefully given prior right hepatectomy.

B. Peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (220 ng/mL) and early recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the 2 lesions of segments II and III aiming for R0 margins.
• Avoid any formal left hepatectomy or extended resection.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of left R0 hepatectomy for liver metastases three years ago. CEA 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VIII (3.8 cm) in contact with the IVC. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Deep solitary recurrence, technical assessment of resection required.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Single hepatic lesion, 3.8 cm, confined to segment VIII – meets the size and number criteria for hepatic resection.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; CEA is markedly elevated, suggesting active disease but not yet proven disseminated spread.  
  • Prior left hepatectomy leaves a right‑lobe remnant; removal of segment VIII would preserve segments V, VI, VII, likely providing an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) if volumetry confirms >30 % of total liver volume in a non‑cirrhotic liver.  
  • Tumor contacts the IVC, representing a technical challenge; however, IVC involvement can be managed with vascular control, limited IVC resection, or patch repair in experienced centers, making resection feasible pending detailed vascular assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging and functional assessment  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis and repeat liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to confirm solitary disease and delineate IVC involvement.  
   – Obtain liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance, and volumetric CT to calculate FLR.  
   – Rationale: ensures no occult extra‑hepatic metastases and confirms that the liver reserve can tolerate resection.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Initiate a 2–3‑month regimen of FOLFOX (or FOLFIRI) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status.  
   – Rationale: down‑size the tumor, test biologic aggressiveness, and potentially increase the chance of an R0 margin while preserving hepatic parenchyma.  

C. Re‑assessment of resectability after systemic therapy  
   – Repeat imaging to evaluate tumor response and IVC involvement; repeat FLR calculation.  
   – If the lesion remains resectable with an anticipated negative margin, proceed to surgery.  

D. Surgical intervention  
   – Perform a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of segment VIII with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance.  
   – If IVC involvement persists, consider limited IVC wedge resection with primary repair or patch angioplasty; employ total hepatic vascular exclusion or selective inflow/outflow control as needed.  
   – Aim for R0 resection while preserving segments V, VI, VII to maintain adequate liver function.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic therapy (same regimen or alternative based on response) for 3–6 months.  
   – Schedule serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first two years.
Reference:

A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform expert liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to precisely evaluate the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and right hepatic vein.

• Given the elevated CEA (180 ng/mL) and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status) may be considered to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing mandatory)
• If resectability is confirmed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 65 years old, right hepatectomy for metastases in 2022. Surveillance: CEA 150 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.3 and 3.1 cm). BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Late liver recurrence, no other locations, satisfactory liver volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable (potentially resectable but with high confidence for curative resection).  
- Rationale:  
  • Two isolated hepatic lesions, both ≤3.5 cm, located in segments II and III, amenable to an anatomic left lateral segmentectomy or limited wedge resections.  
  • No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease on the provided imaging.  
  • Prior right hepatectomy leaves a left liver remnant; the remaining liver volume is reported as satisfactory, suggesting an adequate future liver remnant (FLR > 30 % of total liver volume) for additional resection.  
  • BRAF wild‑type status indicates a more favorable biology compared with BRAF‑mutated disease.  
  • CEA is markedly elevated (150 ng/mL), but this alone does not preclude resection; it underscores the need for systemic therapy but does not affect technical resectability.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 2–3 months of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab)  
   – Rationale: Treat occult micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology/response, and potentially down‑size lesions; high CEA suggests aggressive disease.  

B. Restaging imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT of the liver, plus CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) after chemotherapy  
   – Rationale: Confirm that disease remains confined to the liver and that lesions remain resectable; detect any new extra‑hepatic sites.  

C. Surgical resection – left lateral segmentectomy (anatomic removal of segments II and III) with negative margins (R0)  
   – Rationale: Curative intent; anatomic resection provides oncologic clearance while preserving segment IV for adequate FLR. Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and exclude additional occult lesions.  

D. Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (3–6 months, regimen based on response and prior exposure)  
   – Rationale: Reduce risk of further recurrence given prior hepatic recurrence and elevated CEA; standard of care for resected colorectal liver metastases after recurrence.  

E. Surveillance – CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for at least 3 years.  
   – Rationale: Early detection of further recurrence, especially given prior hepatic relapse.
Reference:

Response:

The patient is potentially resectable. Rationale:  
- Disease is limited to two hepatic lesions (segment IVa 2.6 cm, segment VIII 1.9 cm) with no extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic CT.  
- Total tumor burden is low (<5 cm cumulative) and both lesions are amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resection/ablation.  
- Prior bisegmentectomy V‑VI leaves a remaining liver that, in a non‑cirrhotic liver, is expected to provide an adequate future liver remnant (FLR > 30 % of total liver volume) provided that resection is limited to segment IVa and segment VIII.  
- Absence of major vascular or biliary invasion on the current MRI.  
- High CEA and KRAS mutation do not preclude resection but warrant systemic therapy to assess tumor biology.

   • Regimen: FOLFOX (or FOLFIRI) + bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated status.  
   • Rationale: Treat occult micrometastases, assess disease biology, and potentially downsize lesions to facilitate a less extensive hepatic operation.  

B. Restaging work‑up  
   • Repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted imaging) and CT chest/abdomen after chemotherapy.  
   • Volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR after planned resection.  
   • Rationale: Confirm that lesions remain resectable and that FLR is sufficient; detect any new extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Definitive hepatic treatment (once disease is stable or responding)  
   • Preferred: Combined approach – anatomical resection of segment IVa (central hepatectomy) plus percutaneous image‑guided microwave ablation of the segment VIII lesion.  
   • Alternative (if volumetry shows adequate FLR): simultaneous anatomical resections of segments IVa and VIII.  
   • Rationale: Achieve R0 clearance while preserving maximal parenchyma; ablation is especially useful for the right‑anterior lesion to avoid a larger right‑sided resection that could jeopardize FLR.  

D. Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic therapy  
   • Resume the same chemotherapy backbone for an additional 4–6 months, adjusting based on postoperative recovery and pathology (margin status, response).  
   • Rationale: Consolidate local control and address microscopic disease, especially given the high pre‑operative CEA.

Case_Content:
Woman, 61 years old, extended right hepatectomy performed three years earlier. Surveillance: CEA 360 ng/mL. Liver MRI: single metastasis segment III (3.8 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, potentially resectable depending on future liver remnant.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Single 3.8 cm metastasis confined to segment III, the only remaining hepatic segment after an extended right hepatectomy.  
  • No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
  • Resectability hinges on the future liver remnant (FLR); if the left lateral sector (segments II‑IV) can provide ≥30 % of total liver volume (or ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is present) and there is no portal hypertension, a curative resection is feasible.  
  • KRAS mutation does not preclude surgery but influences systemic therapy choice.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced CT volumetry or MRI‑based liver volumetry to quantify FLR.  
   - Assess liver functional reserve (ICG clearance, LiMAx, or 99mTc‑mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy).  
   - Evaluate for portal hypertension (platelet count, spleen size, Doppler US).  
   - Review performance status, comorbidities, and prior chemotherapy exposure.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate 2–3 months of FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOX) plus bevacizumab, given KRAS mutation and elevated CEA, to test tumor biology and potentially downsize the lesion.  
   - Re‑image after therapy to confirm disease stability or response and to reassess FLR.  

C. Surgical intervention (contingent on step A/B results)  
   - If FLR is adequate (≥30 % functional liver) after neoadjuvant therapy, proceed with a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of segment III, preserving segments II and IV.  
   - If FLR is borderline, perform pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) of the left portal branches to induce hypertrophy of the remaining left lobe, then repeat volumetry and proceed to segmentectomy once safe FLR is achieved.  
   - In the rare event that FLR remains insufficient despite PVE, consider ALPPS or non‑surgical ablative options (RFA/MWA) as alternatives.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance bevacizumab) for 3–6 months as adjuvant treatment, guided by pathology (margin status, tumor regression grade).  
   - Implement intensive surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, history of segment VII resection. Liver MRI: local recurrence at resection site (2.5 cm) and additional nodule segment V. No other lesion at the thoraco CT scan CEA 410 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Localized recurrence on resection scar, complex technical feasibility.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Two hepatic lesions (2.5 cm recurrence at prior segment VII scar and a second nodule in segment V) with no extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑CT.  
  • Both lesions are amenable to anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing resection provided that the future liver remnant (FLR) meets age‑adjusted functional thresholds (≥40 % for a 71‑year‑old).  
  • Prior right‑posterior (segment VII) resection reduces residual volume; therefore volumetric and functional assessment is required to confirm that sufficient FLR will remain after repeat hepatectomy.  
  • No contraindicating factors (e.g., uncontrolled comorbidity, severe liver dysfunction) have been reported, but these must be verified.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative work‑up – Obtain liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR), indocyanine‑green clearance, and a contrast‑enhanced CT volumetry to calculate FLR. Assess performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and tumor biology (KRAS/BRAF, MSI). Rationale: to confirm surgical candidacy and plan extent of resection or need for hypertrophy.  

B. If FLR ≥40 % and liver function adequate – Proceed to a single‑stage, parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy:  
   – Segment V anatomical resection (or wedge with ≥1 cm margin).  
   – Wide‑margin excision of the recurrent nodule at the segment VII scar (segmentectomy or non‑anatomic resection).  
   Rationale: Achieves R0 resection of all hepatic disease while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.  

C. If FLR <40 % or borderline liver function – Implement a staged hypertrophy strategy:  
   – Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches (including segment V territory) to induce left‑lobe hypertrophy.  
   – Re‑assess FLR after 4–6 weeks; if adequate, proceed with the combined segment V + segment VII resection as in step B.  
   Rationale: Increases safe resection volume and reduces postoperative liver failure risk.  

D. If patient is unfit for surgery or hypertrophy fails – Consider non‑surgical alternatives:  
   – Percutaneous image‑guided ablation (RFA/MWA) of both lesions, preferably with a margin‑enhancing technique.  
   – Systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) with or without targeted agents, aiming for disease control and possible conversion to resectability.  
   Rationale: Provides oncologic control while avoiding the morbidity of an extensive hepatectomy in a high‑risk individual.

Case_Content:
Woman, 55 years old, history of left hepatectomy for synchronous metastases. Surveillance: CEA 560 ng/mL. Liver MRI: multiple lesions in right and left lobes (up to 4.5 cm). RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Diffuse liver recurrence, potentially non-curative.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Current classification: potentially resectable but not immediately resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Bilobar disease with multiple lesions up to 4.5 cm in both right and residual left liver segments after a prior left hepatectomy limits the achievable future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • Standard oncologic criteria require complete removal of all macroscopic disease with negative margins and an FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % after chemotherapy) in a non‑cirrhotic liver. The present distribution of lesions would leave an FLR below these thresholds without further hypertrophy.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but the extent of intra‑hepatic burden suggests that conversion strategies (systemic down‑staging, portal vein embolization, or staged hepatectomy) are needed before a curative resection can be contemplated.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion therapy – Initiate first‑line chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or FOLFOX + anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS‑wild type) for 2–3 months.  
   • Goal: tumor shrinkage, control of micrometastatic disease, and assessment of tumor biology.  

B. Restaging and volumetric assessment – Repeat contrast‑enhanced MRI (or CT) and calculate FLR volume after systemic therapy.  
   • Determine whether disease burden has decreased sufficiently and whether FLR meets the ≥30–40 % threshold.  

C. Hypertrophy induction (if FLR inadequate) – If FLR remains suboptimal but disease is otherwise resectable, proceed with portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be preserved, or consider ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy is required and patient fitness permits.  
   • Aim: increase FLR to safe volume while maintaining oncologic control.  

D. Surgical resection – Once adequate FLR is achieved and disease is confined to the liver, perform an anatomic curative resection (e.g., right trisectionectomy or extended right hepatectomy) with negative margins.  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance; consider intra‑operative ablation for borderline lesions if needed.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Resume postoperative systemic treatment (same regimen or maintenance) for at least 6 months, followed by regular CEA and imaging surveillance.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver recurrences (up to 4.5 cm) after a prior left hepatectomy, without reported extrahepatic disease. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution in a previously reduced liver, and multiplicity of lesions make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and anatomical assessment
• Given the high CEA level (560 ng/mL) and multifocal recurrence, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is disease control rather than immediate curative intent.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.

C. Consideration of selective local treatment only if major response occurs
• If significant tumor downsizing occurs, reassess feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections or ablative strategies for dominant lesions.
• Any surgical consideration would be secondary to systemic disease control.

D. If disease remains diffuse
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• If disease remains diffuse, consider palliative or symptom-oriented local approaches as appropriate.

   – Rationale: Ensures postoperative liver safety while still achieving local control.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of planned 6‑month regimen) based on pathology (margin status, response).  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.

   – Initiate 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX (± bevacizumab) given BRAF wild‑type status and presumed KRAS/NRAS wild‑type; adjust based on molecular profile if available.

   – Rationale: achieves R0 clearance while preserving maximal functional liver tissue; minimally invasive approach reduces morbidity and facilitates rapid recovery.

   – Resume systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of FOLFOX or switch to CAPOX) for a total of 6 months peri‑operatively, tailored to response and tolerance.
