Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, operated two years earlier with a left hepatectomy.Liver MRI: recurrence segment VIII (3.1 cm) in contact with the middle hepatic vein. CEA 200 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Isolated complex recurrence of the hepatic dome, technical assessment required.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Single hepatic recurrence, 3.1 cm, confined to segment VIII.  
  • Prior left hepatectomy leaves a right‑liver remnant (segments V–VIII) that can generally provide an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) if a limited segmental resection is performed.  
  • The lesion contacts the middle hepatic vein; preservation or limited resection of this vein is technically feasible in experienced centers, allowing a parenchymal‑sparing approach.  
  • No reported extra‑hepatic disease; CEA is markedly elevated, suggesting aggressive biology but not a contraindication to resection.  
  • Resectability hinges on confirming sufficient FLR volume, preserved liver function, and the ability to achieve negative margins without compromising venous outflow.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and comprehensive imaging  
   – Perform triphasic contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, pelvis and PET‑CT to rule out occult extra‑hepatic metastases and to delineate vascular anatomy of the middle hepatic vein.  
   – Rationale: Confirm isolated hepatic disease and plan the extent of vascular control.  

B. Functional and volumetric liver assessment  
   – Obtain liver function tests, Child‑Pugh score, indocyanine green (ICG) clearance, and CT‑based volumetry of the future liver remnant.  
   – Rationale: Ensure FLR >30 % (or >40 % if underlying liver disease) and adequate functional reserve to tolerate resection.  

C. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Initiate a modern oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months, with serial CEA and imaging to assess response.  
   – Rationale: Treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially downsize the lesion to facilitate a margin‑negative resection.  

D. Surgical resection (post‑neoadjuvant assessment)  
   – If FLR and response are satisfactory, proceed with a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy or wedge resection of segment VIII, aiming for R0 margins.  
   – Preserve the middle hepatic vein when possible; if resection is required, consider venous reconstruction (e.g., interposition graft) or limited resection with adequate outflow from remaining segments.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and vascular relationships.  
   – Rationale: Achieve curative intent while minimizing loss of functional liver parenchyma.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume systemic therapy (adjuvant or continuation of pre‑operative regimen) based on pathology (margin status, response) and molecular profile.  
   – Schedule surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver recurrence in segment VIII (3.1 cm) after a prior left hepatectomy, without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesion is located in the hepatic dome and in contact with the middle hepatic vein, in the only remaining right liver. Although technically demanding, a parenchymal-sparing resection preserving venous outflow may be feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of previous major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable, pending precise vascular and volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform expert liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define the exact relationship of the lesion to the middle hepatic vein and right hepatic vein.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and assess venous outflow preservation.

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (200 ng/mL) and delay of recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered to assess tumor biology and treat micrometastatic disease.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.

D. Surgical management (strict parenchymal-sparing)
• If resectability is confirmed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII.
• Particular attention must be paid to preserving the middle hepatic vein or planning a limited venous resection/reconstruction if required.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both approaches.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if administered.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.

  • Single hepatic lesion, 3.9 cm, confined to segment VII, no extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  • Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V leaves sufficient future liver remnant (segments II, III, VI, VIII, and left lateral sector) to safely tolerate a limited segmentectomy.  
  • Anatomically approachable lesion permits an anatomic segmentectomy with anticipated R0 margins.  
  • No reported portal hypertension, adequate performance status presumed, and no contraindicating comorbidities mentioned.

   - Obtain liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan, and volumetric CT/MRI to confirm FLR >30 % of total liver volume.  
   - Review prior pathology (margin status of the initial resection) and assess disease‑free interval.  
   - Multidisciplinary confirmation of resectability and discussion of peri‑operative chemotherapy options.  

B. Systemic therapy (optional)  
   - Given a late isolated recurrence (>12 months disease‑free) and clear resectability, proceed directly to surgery; reserve peri‑operative chemotherapy for high‑risk features (e.g., high CEA, multiple prior recurrences).

   - Perform an anatomic segmentectomy of segment VII using intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate margins.  
   - Aim for ≥1 cm negative margin (R0).

D. Post‑operative oncologic management  
   - Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, acknowledging KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
   - Schedule surveillance imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then semi‑annually, with concurrent CEA monitoring.

Case_Content:
Man, 72 years old, right hepatectomy 4 years ago. Current liver MRI: multiple nodules segment III, 1-2 cm. CEA 550 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Multifocal recurrence, assessment of resectability and local alternatives.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • The only radiographic disease described is multiple 1‑2 cm nodules confined to segment III of the left liver, which is amenable to a parenchymal‑sparing resection (segment III wedge or segmentectomy) while preserving segments II and IV as future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • Prior right hepatectomy leaves a left‑lateral liver; the remaining volume is likely sufficient for safe resection provided that FLR is >30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver and that liver function is preserved.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, but this has not been formally excluded; absence of such disease is a prerequisite for curative intent.  
  • RAS wild‑type status supports the use of systemic therapy and does not preclude surgery.  
  • High CEA (550 ng/mL) raises concern for aggressive biology; this favors neoadjuvant systemic therapy to test disease kinetics before committing to surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Obtain contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis, PET‑CT if available, and full liver function panel (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets, ICG clearance).  
   - Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR after a hypothetical segment III resection.  
   - Rationale: Confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease, quantify liver reserve, and ensure patient fitness for major surgery.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate a standard first‑line regimen for RAS‑wild‑type metastatic colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOX ± panitumumab or bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
   - Rationale: Assess tumor biology, potentially downsize lesions, and treat micrometastatic disease; high CEA suggests aggressive disease that benefits from systemic control before surgery.  

C. Re‑assessment for curative‑intent surgery  
   - Repeat liver MRI after systemic therapy to evaluate response of segment III lesions.  
   - If disease remains confined to segment III and FLR is adequate, proceed with a parenchymal‑sparing resection (segment III wedge/segmentectomy) or percutaneous ablative therapy (RFA/MWA) if resection would compromise liver volume.  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 resection while preserving liver function; ablative therapy is an alternative when resection margin concerns exist.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   - Pathology review for margin status and tumor response.  
   - Consider adjuvant chemotherapy based on final pathology and response to neoadjuvant therapy.  
   - Implement a surveillance protocol (CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging every 6 months for the first 2 years).

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer with three liver metastases (2-4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 620 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Synchronous hepato-pulmonary involvement, discussion of sequential strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Three hepatic metastases 2‑4 cm each – size and number are within criteria for hepatic resection provided adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • Bilateral pulmonary nodules – extra‑hepatic disease is limited and potentially amenable to metastasectomy; presence of resectable lung disease does not automatically preclude curative intent.  
  • No reported involvement of major hepatic vasculature or biliary structures; however, precise segmental location and proximity to portal/hepatic veins are unknown and will determine need for parenchymal‑sparing techniques or portal vein embolization.  
  • KRAS mutation and markedly elevated CEA (620 ng/mL) suggest aggressive biology; therefore systemic therapy is required to assess tumor response before committing to surgery.  
  • Overall, the disease burden meets criteria for a “potentially resectable” scenario pending response to neoadjuvant therapy and confirmation of sufficient FLR and pulmonary reserve.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (6–8 cycles)  
   - Preferred regimen: FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab (or cetuximab if RAS wild‑type, but KRAS mutated precludes EGFR‑targeted agents).  
   - Goal: tumor down‑staging, assess biological behavior, and reduce CEA.  

B. Restaging imaging after induction  
   - Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast for volumetry and lesion response.  
   - High‑resolution chest CT to re‑evaluate pulmonary nodules.  
   - Decision point: if all lesions show ≥30 % shrinkage or become resectable, proceed to surgical planning; if progression, consider alternative systemic options or palliative approach.  

C. Surgical sequencing (multidisciplinary consensus)  
   1. Liver‑first approach (if FLR ≥30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver or can be increased with portal vein embolization).  
      - Perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (e.g., segmental/sectional resections) aiming for R0 margins.  
      - Consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization if FLR insufficient.  
   2. Pulmonary metastasectomy (within 4–6 weeks after hepatic resection, provided adequate recovery).  
      - Video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) for peripheral nodules; open resection for central lesions.  
   - Rationale: liver disease is the dominant determinant of survival; addressing it first reduces risk of hepatic failure and allows assessment of postoperative hepatic function before lung surgery.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., fluoropyrimidine‑based) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, tailored to pathologic response and residual disease.  
   - Consider enrollment in clinical trial or use of anti‑angiogenic maintenance (bevacizumab) if tolerated.  

E. Surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
Reference:

The patient presents with three liver metastases (2–4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules in the setting of a left T4N2 colon cancer, without other reported sites. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically resectable. This situation is considered potentially resectable in a multimodal, sequential curative strategy, provided both hepatic and pulmonary disease are amenable to complete treatment.

• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon primary) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

	2.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• The sequence (liver-first vs lung-first) depends on response and technical considerations.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma, four liver metastases (1.5-3.8 cm) and nodular peritoneal involvement at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal disease, not curable upfront, discussion of induction chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Unresectable at presentation.  
- Rationale:  
  • Presence of nodular peritoneal involvement represents extra‑hepatic disease, which by current colorectal liver metastasis guidelines precludes curative‑intent liver resection unless all peritoneal disease can be completely eradicated.  
  • Four hepatic lesions (1.5–3.8 cm) are technically resectable in isolation, but simultaneous peritoneal carcinomatosis makes a curative‑intent combined resection unlikely without prior disease down‑staging.  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, distribution of peritoneal nodules, or performance status; therefore a definitive curative operation cannot be planned now.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, guided by molecular profile).  
   - Rationale: Aim to achieve maximal tumor shrinkage, assess tumor biology, and potentially convert both hepatic and peritoneal disease to a resectable state.  

B. Restaging after 2–3 months with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen, PET‑CT if available, and diagnostic laparoscopy to evaluate peritoneal disease (PCI score).  
   - Rationale: Determine radiologic response, re‑assess resectability, and obtain tissue for molecular confirmation if needed.  

C. Multimodal curative intent if conversion achieved:  
   - If imaging shows ≤5 hepatic lesions amenable to a 30 %+ FLR and peritoneal disease limited to a low PCI (≤5–7) with complete cytoreduction feasible, proceed to:  
     • Synchronous or staged right hemicolectomy (if not already resected) + anatomic/segmental liver resections to clear all metastases.  
     • Cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) for peritoneal nodules.  
   - Rationale: Combined resection offers the only chance for long‑term survival when disease is limited and completely removable.  

D. If conversion fails (persistent extensive peritoneal disease or inadequate liver remnant):  
   - Continue systemic therapy, consider clinical trial enrollment, and provide best supportive/palliative care.  
   - Rationale: Curative surgery is not feasible; focus shifts to disease control and quality of life.
Reference:
Step 1 - The patient presents with four liver metastases (1.5–3.8 cm) associated with nodular peritoneal involvement on CT. The presence of peritoneal carcinomatosis indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. According to oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable from a hepatobiliary perspective in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (950 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.
• The goal is to evaluate tumor biology and potential response at both hepatic and peritoneal sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, mid-rectal T3N1 tumor with five bilobar liver metastases and a right lung metastasis at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 330 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, evaluation of a possible combined approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
  • Five bilobar liver metastases can be cleared with an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection provided that a future liver remnant (FLR) of ≥30 % (≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) can be preserved.  
  • Presence of a solitary right‑lung metastasis does not preclude curative intent if the pulmonary lesion is resectable and the patient has adequate pulmonary reserve.  
  • RAS wild‑type status favors use of anti‑EGFR agents to increase response rates, improving the chance of achieving R0 margins.  
  • No information on lesion size, proximity to major vessels, or FLR volume; therefore definitive resectability cannot be confirmed without further imaging and functional assessment.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (2–3 months)  
   – Regimen: FOLFOXIRI + cetuximab (RAS wild‑type) or FOLFOX + cetuximab if concern for toxicity.  
   – Rationale: Maximize tumor shrinkage in liver and lung, treat micrometastatic disease, and allow assessment of biologic behavior.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment (after cycle 4)  
   – Multiphasic liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, high‑resolution chest CT, and volumetric CT to calculate FLR.  
   – Pulmonary function tests (FEV1, DLCO) to confirm operability of lung lesion.  
   – Rationale: Determine response, resectability, and need for adjuncts such as portal vein embolization (PVE).  

C. Surgical planning (based on restaging)  
   – If FLR ≥30 % (or after PVE to achieve adequate FLR) and lung lesion resectable:  
        • Option 1: Simultaneous liver‑and‑lung resection (single operative session) for selected patients with good performance status.  
        • Option 2: Staged approach – first liver resection (major or multiple minor resections) followed by video‑assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection or segmentectomy of the lung lesion 4–6 weeks later.  
   – Rationale: Achieve R0 resection of all macroscopic disease while preserving hepatic and pulmonary function.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   – Resume systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of anti‑EGFR‑containing regimen) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, tailored to pathologic response and tolerance.  
   – Rationale: Reduce risk of recurrence, especially given initial high tumor burden and elevated CEA.  

E. Surveillance  
   – CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT chest/abdomen) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases and a single right lung metastasis in the setting of a mid-rectal T3N1 tumor, without other reported sites. Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not contraindicate a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease may be amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections provided adequate future liver remnant is preserved. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.
• Pelvic MRI to integrate rectal treatment planning.
• Given the high CEA level (330 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.
• Continue systemic third-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, left colon cancer with six liver metastases and lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 780 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Liver involvement associated with extra-hepatic lymph nodes, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Six hepatic lesions do not per se preclude resection; modern hepatectomy can address multiple metastases provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • Presence of a hepatic‑pedicle lymph node represents extra‑hepatic disease, but isolated regional nodal metastasis can be surgically removed in experienced centers; therefore it does not automatically render the case unresectable.  
  • No information is given about the size, distribution (unilobar vs bilobar), or proximity of the lesions to major vascular structures, which are critical to determine whether an R0 liver resection with clear margins is technically feasible.  
  • KRAS mutation and markedly elevated CEA indicate aggressive biology but are not absolute contraindications to surgery; they do, however, increase the importance of achieving disease‑free margins and of systemic disease control.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab).  
   - Goal: tumor down‑staging, assessment of biologic behavior, and potential conversion of borderline lesions to resectable status.  

B. Restaging after 2–3 months with high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI and PET‑CT if needed.  
   - Evaluate response of liver lesions, size of hepatic‑pedicle node, and calculate FLR.  

C. Pre‑operative optimization (if FLR <30 % of total liver volume).  
   - Consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to hypertrophy the future liver remnant.  

D. Surgical phase (performed once adequate FLR and disease control are confirmed):  
   - Stage 1 – Resection of the primary left‑sided colon cancer (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
   - Stage 2 – Hepatic resection tailored to lesion distribution (e.g., extended right or left hepatectomy, or combined anatomical and non‑anatomical resections) aiming for R0 margins; simultaneous removal of the hepatic‑pedicle lymph node(s) with a formal hepatic‑pedicle lymphadenectomy.  
   - The sequence (simultaneous vs staged) should be decided based on intra‑operative assessment, patient fitness, and extent of liver resection.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy (post‑operative) tailored to KRAS‑mutated biology, possibly incorporating anti‑EGFR agents if later molecular profiling permits, and continued surveillance with serial CEA and imaging.

This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable from a hepatobiliary perspective.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions and other para-aortic enlarged lymph nodes
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab;
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and abdominal CT after 2–3 months to reassess liver disease and nodal involvement.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (highly exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in case of major response with major regression of nodal disease and significant downsizing of liver lesions.
• Any surgical strategy would remain highly selected and dependent on sustained disease control.

E. Surgical management of liver metastases (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections or ablation guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Perform en-bloc lymphadenectomy of the hepatic pedicles 
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis at the total body CT scan. CEA 860 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Systemic disease with brain involvement, neurological priority indication.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline) – The liver disease is multiple and bilobar, which exceeds the typical criteria for immediate curative hepatectomy (≤4 lesions, unilobar or amenable to two‑stage resection with adequate future liver remnant). However, conversion to resectability is possible after systemic therapy and/or liver‑directed interventions. The presence of a solitary cerebellar metastasis represents extra‑hepatic disease that must be controlled first; it does not automatically preclude hepatic resection if the brain lesion can be treated effectively.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neuro‑oncologic control – Immediate stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) or surgical resection of the cerebellar metastasis, depending on size, symptomatic status, and accessibility. Rationale: brain disease is the current priority; local control prevents neurologic decline and allows systemic therapy to proceed safely.  
B. Systemic induction therapy – Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) combined with molecular‑targeted agents based on KRAS/NRAS/BRAF/MSI status. Rationale: aim to achieve tumor shrinkage in both colon primary and liver metastases, and to assess disease biology.  
C. Re‑assessment of hepatic burden – After 2–3 cycles (≈8–12 weeks), repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with volumetry. Evaluate response, calculate future liver remnant (FLR), and consider portal vein embolization (PVE) if FLR is insufficient. Rationale: determine whether a curative‑intent hepatic resection is feasible.  
D. Curative‑intent liver surgery – If imaging shows sufficient down‑staging (≤3‑4 lesions confined to one or two segments) and FLR ≥ 30 % (≥40 % if steatosis or chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), proceed with either a single‑stage anatomical resection or a two‑stage/ALPPS approach as dictated by lesion distribution. Rationale: achieve R0 resection of all hepatic disease after extra‑hepatic disease is controlled.  
E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy – Post‑operative systemic therapy tailored to molecular profile, with consideration of immunotherapy if MSI‑high. Rationale: eradicate microscopic residual disease and reduce recurrence risk.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, rectosigmoid tumor, four liver metastases and pelvic peritoneal implants at the abdominal CT scan. BRAF wild-type, CEA 320 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal involvement, possible multimodal strategy to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
   Four hepatic metastases – resectability depends on their segmental distribution, size, and ability to achieve an R0 resection with a future liver remnant (FLR) ≥30 % (≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury).  
   Presence of pelvic peritoneal implants – may be amenable to cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with HIPEC if the peritoneal cancer index (PCI) is low and disease is limited to resectable sites.  
   BRAF wild‑type status is favorable for response to modern systemic regimens.  
   Elevated CEA (320 ng/mL) indicates high tumor burden but does not preclude resection after down‑staging.  
   Without data on lesion location, FLR, liver function, and PCI, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed; therefore the case is considered potentially resectable pending further assessment and neoadjuvant therapy response.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX + anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type).  
   - Rationale: Aim to downsize hepatic lesions, treat occult micrometastases, and assess tumor biology; high CEA suggests aggressive disease that benefits from early systemic control.  

B. Restaging after 2–3 months with contrast‑enhanced liver MRI, high‑resolution CT, and diagnostic laparoscopy to:  
   - Re‑evaluate hepatic lesion number, size, and resectability; calculate FLR; assess liver parenchymal quality.  
   - Determine peritoneal disease burden (PCI) and feasibility of complete cytoreduction.  

C. Multidisciplinary surgical planning based on restaging:  
   If hepatic disease becomes resectable and PCI ≤10–12  
   - Option 1 (simultaneous approach): One‑stage combined liver resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing) followed immediately by CRS‑HIPEC for pelvic implants, provided operative time and physiologic reserve allow.  
   - Option 2 (staged approach):  
     1. First stage – liver‑first resection (or two‑stage/ALPPS if FLR insufficient).  
     2. Second stage – after hepatic recovery (4–6 weeks), perform CRS‑HIPEC targeting peritoneal disease.  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 resection of all macroscopic disease while preserving liver function and minimizing peri‑operative morbidity.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy (continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance bevacizumab/anti‑EGFR) for at least 6 months post‑surgery, followed by regular surveillance (CEA, imaging every 3–6 months).  

E. If restaging shows persistent unresectable liver disease or high PCI (>12)  
   - Continue systemic therapy, consider enrollment in clinical trials (e.g., targeted agents, immunotherapy if MSI‑H), and reassess resectability at later intervals.

Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon primary) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 66 years old, T3N1M1 transverse colon cancer, five liver metastases and two pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 420 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilateral hepato-pulmonary involvement, potentially treatable sequentially.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Five hepatic metastases are present, but bilateral distribution does not automatically preclude resection; adequacy of future liver remnant (FLR) and ability to achieve R0 margins are the decisive factors, which are not yet quantified.  
  • Two pulmonary nodules represent limited extra‑hepatic disease; if they are ≤5 cm total and amenable to metastasectomy or ablative therapy, they do not render the case unresectable.  
  • RAS wild‑type status favors response to conversion chemotherapy and possible use of anti‑EGFR agents, supporting a curative intent.  
  • No data on FLR volume, liver function, or pulmonary reserve; therefore definitive resectability cannot be confirmed at this stage.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy – Start a 3‑month regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± cetuximab) to downsize hepatic and pulmonary lesions and assess tumor biology.  
   • Rationale: High CEA and multiple metastases indicate aggressive disease; conversion chemotherapy can increase the chance of achieving an R0 liver resection and may eradicate or shrink lung nodules.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment – After induction, obtain contrast‑enhanced liver MRI, high‑resolution chest CT, and volumetric liver CT to calculate FLR; perform pulmonary function tests and assess performance status.  
   • Rationale: Determines whether a single‑stage hepatectomy is feasible, or whether portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage approach is required; also confirms resectability of lung lesions.  

C. Optimization of hepatic reserve – If FLR <30 % (in a normal liver) or <40 % (in a steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured liver), proceed with right (or left) portal vein embolization or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
   • Rationale: Ensures sufficient postoperative liver function and reduces risk of post‑hepatectomy liver failure.  

D. Surgical resection of liver metastases – Perform curative‑intent hepatectomy (single‑stage if FLR adequate, otherwise staged) aiming for R0 margins; consider intra‑operative ultrasound to locate all lesions and apply radiofrequency ablation for lesions that would otherwise compromise FLR.  
   • Rationale: Achieves complete clearance of intra‑hepatic disease, which is the cornerstone of long‑term survival.  

E. Management of pulmonary metastases – After hepatic surgery and recovery (≈4–6 weeks), reassess lung nodules; proceed with video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) wedge resection or SBRT if lesions are peripheral and ≤3 cm, or consider simultaneous liver‑lung resection only if patient’s physiologic reserve permits and operative time is acceptable.  
   • Rationale: Sequential approach minimizes peri‑operative morbidity; definitive treatment of extra‑hepatic disease is required for cure.  

F. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy – Resume systemic therapy (e.g., fluoropyrimidine ± anti‑EGFR) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, tailored to pathologic response and molecular profile (including BRAF, MSI status).  
   • Rationale: Consolidates response, addresses microscopic residual disease, and improves disease‑free survival.

From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease may be amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections provided an adequate future liver remnant is preserved. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the primary tumor
• Extended right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the lung metastases
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.
• Continue systemic third-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-pulmonary involvement, not resectable upfront.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (conversion‑resectable).  
- Justification:  
  • Six bilobar liver metastases exceed the criteria for upfront resection because an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be assured without pre‑operative hypertrophy or staged approach.  
  • Presence of pulmonary micronodules indicates extra‑hepatic disease; however, isolated limited lung metastases are not an absolute contraindication if they can be controlled with systemic therapy or later metastasectomy.  
  • RAS wild‑type status permits use of anti‑EGFR agents, increasing the likelihood of tumor shrinkage.  
  • No information on FLR volume, liver function, or performance status; therefore, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed at this time, but conversion to resectability is feasible.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion therapy (first 2–3 months)  
   – Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type.  
   – Rationale: maximize tumor response in liver and lung, increase chance of achieving R0 resection and allow FLR hypertrophy strategies later.  

B. Concurrent or sequential neoadjuvant treatment of the rectal primary  
   – Deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy (45‑50 Gy with capecitabine/5‑FU) after the initial systemic cycles, or integrate radiotherapy into the systemic regimen if tolerable.  
   – Rationale: downstage the T4 primary, reduce risk of local recurrence, and synchronize timing with hepatic treatment.  

C. Restaging and multidisciplinary reassessment (after 2–3 months)  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI, high‑resolution chest CT or PET‑CT, and assess FLR volumetry.  
   – Rationale: determine degree of response, re‑evaluate resectability of liver lesions, and decide on need for portal vein embolization (PVE) or two‑stage hepatectomy.  

D. Hepatic surgical plan (if criteria met)

   – Rationale: achieve complete (R0) clearance of liver disease while preserving hepatic function.  

E. Definitive rectal surgery (post‑hepatectomy)  
   – Perform total mesorectal excision (TME) with sphincter‑preserving or abdominoperineal approach based on tumor response and location.  
   – Rationale: curative resection of the primary after systemic disease control.  

F. Management of pulmonary metastases  
   – If residual lung nodules are ≤5 mm and limited in number, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or wedge resection after hepatic and rectal surgeries.  
   – Rationale: eradicate remaining extra‑hepatic disease to complete curative intent.  

G. Adjuvant systemic therapy (post‑operative)  
   – Continue maintenance chemotherapy ± targeted agent for 3–6 months, guided by postoperative pathology and response.  
   – Rationale: reduce risk of recurrence in micrometastatic sites.

• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

H. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• If resection, analysis ofpathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
