• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left colon cancer, liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) and confirmed right iliac bone metastasis at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Hepatic disease: lesions in segments IV, V, VIII are limited to one lobe and could be removed with an extended right hepatectomy or combined segmental resections, provided the future liver remnant (FLR) is ≥30 % of functional liver. → Potentially resectable from a liver‑only perspective.  
- Extra‑hepatic disease: confirmed right iliac bone metastasis. Bone metastasis is not amenable to curative surgical resection and indicates systemic spread. → Overall disease considered unresectable for curative intent.  
- KRAS mutation: precludes anti‑EGFR therapy but does not affect technical resectability.  
Classification: Hepatic lesions are potentially resectable; however, the presence of an untreated bone metastasis makes the patient overall unresectable for a definitive cure at this time.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction therapy – Start a KRAS‑mutated colorectal regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX + bevacizumab). Rationale: down‑size liver lesions, control bone disease, and assess tumor biology.  
B. Radiologic reassessment (≈8‑12 weeks) – Repeat contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI of the liver, PET‑CT or bone scan for the iliac lesion, and calculate FLR volume. Rationale: determine response, re‑evaluate resectability, and decide on need for portal vein embolization (PVE) if FLR insufficient.  
C. Local treatment of bone metastasis – If the iliac lesion remains solitary and symptomatic, deliver stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or conventional external‑beam radiotherapy. Rationale: achieve local control and potentially convert to a “oligometastatic” state.  
D. Surgical resection of liver metastases – If imaging shows adequate tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥30 % (or after PVE to augment FLR), proceed with anatomic resection of segments IV, V, VIII (extended right hepatectomy) or parenchymal‑sparing resections as appropriate. Rationale: achieve R0 hepatic clearance while preserving liver function.  
E. Adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy – Resume or continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., maintenance capecitabine ± bevacizumab) post‑operatively for at least 6 months. Rationale: treat micrometastatic disease and reduce recurrence risk.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with liver metastases in segments IV, V, and VIII associated with a confirmed right iliac bone metastasis in the context of a left colon cancer. The presence of osseous metastatic disease indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control.

B. Management of bone metastasis
• Integrate radiotherapy and/or orthopedic evaluation for the right iliac lesion depending on symptoms and fracture risk.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform periodic liver MRI and whole-body imaging to monitor response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Role of liver-directed therapy
• Liver surgery is not indicated unless an exceptional systemic response with control of bone disease occurs, which remains unlikely.

E. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T3N1 rectal tumor with two liver metastases and an isolated left pulmonary nodule at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 210 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, possibility of a combined approach depending on response.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Two hepatic metastases – number within accepted limits for curative intent (≤3 lesions).  
  • No description of bilobar disease or proximity to major vascular inflow/outflow; assume lesions amenable to R0 resection pending volumetric analysis.  
  • Isolated left pulmonary nodule – solitary extra‑hepatic disease that can be addressed surgically or with stereotactic radiotherapy if resectable.  
  • RAS wild‑type status supports responsiveness to modern systemic regimens, increasing likelihood of conversion to resectability.  
  • Adequate future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be confirmed without volumetry; therefore resectability remains conditional on FLR ≥30 % (normal liver) or ≥40 % (post‑chemotherapy).  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (total neoadjuvant approach)  
   - Initiate 6–8 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type, aiming for maximal tumor shrinkage in liver and lung and early treatment of micrometastatic disease.  
   - Rationale: Improves resection rates, allows assessment of tumor biology, and may downsize lesions to facilitate margin‑negative surgery.  

B. Concurrent neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the rectal primary  
   - Deliver long‑course pelvic radiotherapy with capecitabine (or 5‑FU) during systemic therapy or sequentially, followed by a 6‑8 week interval.  
   - Rationale: Standard of care for T3 rectal cancer to achieve downstaging and reduce local recurrence; synchronizing with systemic therapy optimizes overall treatment time.  

C. Restaging and multidisciplinary reassessment  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, high‑resolution chest CT or PET‑CT, and liver volumetry.  
   - Evaluate FLR, lesion response (RECIST), and pulmonary nodule characteristics.  
   - Rationale: Determines whether curative resection is now feasible and informs need for portal vein embolization (PVE) or alternative local therapies.  

D. Surgical phase (tailored to response)  
   - If liver FLR is adequate and margins can be achieved:  
     • Proceed with anatomical or non‑anatomical liver resection of all metastases (potentially staged with PVE if FLR insufficient).  
     • Consider simultaneous wedge resection of the left pulmonary nodule during the same operative session if patient’s cardiopulmonary reserve permits; otherwise schedule video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) within 4–6 weeks of hepatic resection.  
   - After hepatic (and pulmonary) surgery, complete rectal resection (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) after a further 6‑8 week interval, provided oncologic timing is respected.  
   - Rationale: Prioritizes removal of systemic disease (liver ± lung) while allowing optimal healing before pelvic surgery; simultaneous liver‑lung resection can reduce overall treatment time in selected fit patients.  

E. Adjuvant considerations  
   - Post‑operative systemic therapy (e.g., additional cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to complete a total of 12 months of chemotherapy.  
   - Close surveillance with serial CEA and imaging every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases and a single left pulmonary nodule in the setting of a T3N1 rectal tumor, without other reported sites. Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not preclude a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.
• Pelvic MRI to integrate rectal treatment planning.
• Given the high CEA level (210 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation depending on response pattern.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable after down‑staging (not immediately resectable).  
- Justification:  
  • Eight bilobar liver metastases exceed the typical criteria for a single‑stage curative hepatectomy; achieving an R0 resection would require an insufficient future liver remnant (FLR) without pre‑operative hypertrophy strategies.  
  • Moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis (PCI not quantified) is a contraindication to curative liver resection unless the peritoneal disease can be reduced to a limited burden amenable to cytoreductive surgery + HIPEC.  
  • T4N2 primary tumor with high CEA (970 ng/mL) indicates aggressive biology, further lowering the likelihood of immediate curative surgery.  
  • Therefore, the disease is not resectable at presentation but may become resectable if systemic therapy yields a substantial response in both hepatic and peritoneal sites.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction therapy (2–3 months)  
   - Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with biologic agent selected according to molecular profile (anti‑VEGF if RAS‑mutant, anti‑EGFR if RAS‑wildtype).  
   - Rationale: maximize tumor shrinkage, assess chemosensitivity, and potentially convert lesions to resectable status; also provides early control of micrometastatic disease.  

B. Molecular and functional work‑up (concurrent with A)  
   - Obtain tumor RAS/NRAS, BRAF, and MSI status; assess baseline liver function, bilirubin, albumin, and calculate FLR volume (CT volumetry).  
   - Rationale: guides choice of biologic agent, predicts response, and informs feasibility of future liver‑directed surgery.  

C. Restaging imaging (after 2–3 months of therapy)  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, repeat CT abdomen/pelvis, and consider PET‑CT.  
   - Rationale: quantify response of hepatic and peritoneal disease, re‑calculate PCI, and determine if a curative intent approach is now possible.  

D. Decision node based on restaging  
   - If major response (≥70 % hepatic lesion shrinkage, PCI ≤ 10, FLR ≥ 30 % after planned hypertrophy):  
        • Proceed with a staged liver‑first approach: portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to augment FLR, followed by anatomic resection of remaining disease.  
        • Simultaneously or sequentially address the primary colon tumor (right hemicolectomy) depending on symptomatology and operative risk.  
        • If peritoneal disease remains limited, schedule cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC after hepatic clearance.  
   - If inadequate response (persistent extensive bilobar disease or high PCI):  
        • Continue systemic therapy, consider enrollment in a clinical trial (e.g., immunotherapy for MSI‑high, novel targeted agents).  
        • Maintain best supportive care and reassess periodically; surgery is deferred.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases associated with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (970 ng/mL). The presence of peritoneal dissemination combined with extensive bilobar hepatic disease excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (970 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Five liver metastases are ≤ 3.5 cm and distributed bilobar, which can be addressed with parenchymal‑sparing or staged hepatectomy, satisfying the technical criteria for resection.  
  • Contact of the segment VIII lesion with the middle hepatic vein raises a vascular involvement issue but does not preclude resection; vein resection/reconstruction is feasible.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease beyond the primary colon cancer, fulfilling the oncologic requirement of limited disease.  
  • High CEA (1150 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation indicate aggressive biology, placing the case in the “borderline/biologically high‑risk” category; therefore the disease is not deemed outright resectable without first addressing systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab).  
   - Rationale: Treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially downsize hepatic lesions to facilitate a margin‑negative, parenchymal‑sparing resection.  

B. Restaging after neoadjuvant therapy (contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI of chest, abdomen, pelvis; repeat CEA).  
   - Rationale: Determine response, re‑evaluate resectability, and identify any new extra‑hepatic sites that would alter intent.  

C. Surgical phase (if disease remains resectable):  
   1. Liver‑first approach – perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy targeting all five lesions, preserving ≥ 30 % future liver remnant; address middle hepatic vein involvement with either vein‑preserving technique or limited resection with reconstruction.  
   2. Simultaneous or staged colon resection – based on patient’s physiologic reserve; simultaneous resection is preferred if operative risk is acceptable, otherwise a staged colectomy after hepatic recovery.  
   - Rationale: Prioritizes control of the dominant metastatic burden while minimizing delay to primary tumor removal; preserves hepatic function and allows for R0 margins.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy (post‑operative, 3–6 months, regimen guided by response and tolerability).  
   - Rationale: Consolidate response, address residual microscopic disease, and improve disease‑free survival in high‑risk KRAS‑mutated colorectal cancer.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases (2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 1600 ng/mL. BRAF V600E mutation, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, poor prognosis linked to molecular profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
  • Seven hepatic metastases ranging 2‑5 cm indicate a high tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution, which limits the ability to achieve an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) with a single‑stage resection.  
  • Current hepatobiliary criteria consider resection feasible when an FLR of ≥20‑30 % (in normal liver) can be preserved; without volumetric data the FLR is presumed insufficient.  
  • The absence of documented extra‑hepatic disease keeps the disease confined to the liver, preserving the possibility of conversion to resectability with systemic therapy and/or portal vein embolization (PVE).  
  • Molecular profile (BRAF V600E, MSS) predicts aggressive biology and poorer prognosis, reinforcing the need for a multimodal approach rather than immediate surgery.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with BRAF‑targeted regimen (encorafenib + cetuximab) to achieve tumor shrinkage and assess biologic response.  
   - Rationale: Down‑staging may reduce lesion size/number, improve FLR calculations, and provide early selection of patients with favorable disease kinetics.  

B. Restaging and volumetric assessment (≈8‑12 weeks)  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT with liver volumetry to quantify residual disease and calculate FLR.  
   - Rationale: Objective measurement determines whether a single‑stage resection is possible or if a staged approach is required.  

C. Liver‑directed conversion (if FLR inadequate)  
   - If FLR <30 % after systemic response, proceed with portal vein embolization (right or left depending on planned resection) to induce hypertrophy.  
   - Alternatively, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy is needed and patient fitness permits.  
   - Rationale: Augmenting FLR expands the surgical window while maintaining oncologic clearance.  

D. Curative hepatic resection (post‑PVE or after sufficient down‑staging)  
   - Perform an anatomic resection achieving R0 margins, tailored to the distribution of residual lesions (e.g., right trisectionectomy, extended left hepatectomy, or combined staged resections).  
   - Rationale: Curative intent surgery offers the only chance for long‑term survival in isolated liver disease.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy  
   - Resume BRAF‑targeted therapy ± chemotherapy for 6‑12 months post‑resection, contingent on postoperative recovery and pathology.  
   - Rationale: High recurrence risk associated with BRAF mutation warrants continued systemic control.  

F. Surveillance  
   - Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3‑4 months for the first 2 years, then at increasing intervals.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven liver metastases (2–5 cm) in the setting of a right T4aN2 colon cancer and a BRAF V600E mutation with very high CEA (1600 ng/mL). Despite the disease being confined to the liver, the number of lesions, their size, and especially the unfavorable molecular profile indicate highly aggressive systemic tumor biology. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront, as surgery would not provide meaningful oncologic benefit at this stage.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 7 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (1600 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• The elevated CEA level (1600 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Initiate intensive systemic therapy adapted to the BRAF V600E profile according to MDT decision : give 3-6 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS status is unknow but BRAF V600E profile is poor prognostic factor
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in the rare situation of major radiologic and biologic response with marked reduction in number and size of lesions. 
• In this situation, first multiple atypical resections and ablation guided by ultrasound with the aim to obtain R0 margins.
• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective.

E. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, T3N2 upper rectal cancer with four liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 980 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases with MSI-H profile opening discussion for first-line immunotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Four hepatic metastases are present, but bilobar distribution does not automatically preclude resection if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved (≥30 % of total liver volume in a normal liver, ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is anticipated).  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease other than the primary rectal tumor is reported, satisfying the “no unresectable extra‑hepatic disease” criterion for hepatic resection.  
  • RAS wild‑type and MSI‑high status do not affect technical resectability but influence systemic therapy choice.  
  • Absence of data on lesion size, exact segmental location, liver function (bilirubin, ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh), and volumetric analysis prevents a definitive “resectable” label; therefore the case remains potentially resectable pending further assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the primary rectal tumor  
   - Rationale: T3N2 upper rectal cancer requires down‑staging to improve sphincter‑preserving resection rates and local control; standard long‑course chemoradiation (45‑50 Gy with concurrent 5‑FU or capecitabine) is indicated.  

B. Systemic immunotherapy (first‑line pembrolizumab or nivolumab) for metastatic disease  
   - Rationale: MSI‑high status predicts high response rates to PD‑1 blockade; immunotherapy can achieve rapid tumor shrinkage, potentially converting borderline liver lesions to resectable status and may spare the need for cytotoxic chemotherapy that could impair liver parenchyma.  

C. Restaging after systemic therapy (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT, plus liver volumetry)  
   - Rationale: Evaluate radiologic response of hepatic lesions, calculate FLR, and assess for any new extra‑hepatic sites; decide on need for portal vein embolization (PVE) or two‑stage hepatectomy.  

D. Surgical resection (timing based on restaging)  
   - If FLR ≥30‑40 % and all lesions become resectable:  
     • Option 1 – Simultaneous resection: low anterior resection (or intersphincteric resection if needed) combined with anatomical or non‑anatomical liver resection in a single operation, provided operative risk is acceptable.  
     • Option 2 – Staged approach: first complete rectal resection (allowing pelvic healing), then proceed to liver resection 4‑6 weeks later; preferred if extensive liver surgery is required or if simultaneous surgery would increase morbidity.  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 margins for both primary and metastases, minimize disease recurrence, and align with multidisciplinary consensus for curative intent.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases in the setting of a T3N2 upper rectal cancer. Although technically the liver disease may be amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection, the very high CEA (980 ng/mL) and, most importantly, the MSI-H profile indicate a tumor biology that is highly responsive to immunotherapy. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but surgery is not the first step given the expected efficacy of systemic immunotherapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 4 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (980 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. First-line systemic immunotherapy (mandatory)
• Initiate immunotherapy according to MDT decision as first-line treatment for MSI-H metastatic colorectal cancer.
• The objective is major tumor regression and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical re-evaluation after response
• If a major radiologic response occurs, reassess segmental resectability.
• Plan biopsy of the primary rectal tumor and liver metastases to assess tumor response to immunotherapy
• Consider parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided liver resections only if residual lesions persist and complete clearance is feasible with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic immunotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, two liver metastases segments II and III (3.2 and 4.0 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 320 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 positive.
MDT Discussion: Limited involvement but HER2 mutation may influence systemic therapeutic strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Both hepatic lesions are confined to segments II and III (left lateral section) with diameters of 3.2 cm and 4.0 cm, allowing an anatomic left lateral sectionectomy while preserving adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver).  
  • No radiologic evidence of major vascular invasion, biliary involvement, or extra‑hepatic disease reported.  
  • Primary tumor is resectable (left‑sided colon cancer, T3N1).  
  • The presence of HER2 positivity does not affect anatomic resectability but may influence systemic therapy choice.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (4–6 cycles)  
   - Regimen: HER2‑directed doublet (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab or trastuzumab + lapatinib/tucatinib) combined with a standard fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin backbone (FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
   - Rationale: Down‑size liver lesions, assess tumor biology, and address micrometastatic disease; HER2‑targeted therapy improves response rates in HER2‑positive, BRAF‑wildtype colorectal cancer.  

B. Restaging imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest, abdomen, pelvis) after neoadjuvant therapy  
   - Rationale: Confirm continued resectability, evaluate response, and exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Surgical resection – either simultaneous or staged, based on operative risk and response:  
   - If patient is fit (ECOG 0‑1, adequate hepatic reserve): Simultaneous left hemicolectomy with left lateral sectionectomy.  
   - If concerns about operative time or liver regeneration: Staged approach – first colon resection (standard oncologic left‑sided colectomy), followed 4–6 weeks later by left lateral sectionectomy.  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 resection of both primary and hepatic disease while minimizing peri‑operative morbidity.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy  
   - Continue HER2‑targeted therapy (single‑agent trastuzumab or HER2‑directed maintenance) ± fluoropyrimidine for 6–12 months, guided by pathology (margin status, nodal involvement) and tolerance.  
   - Rationale: Reduce risk of recurrence in high‑risk stage IV disease.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, nine bilobar metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2500 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.Liver  MRI: infiltration of the right portal pedicle.
MDT Discussion: Major liver involvement, vascular invasion compromising resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Current classification: potentially resectable only after down‑staging.  
- Rationale:  
  • Nine bilobar hepatic lesions exceed the typical limit for a single‑stage curative hepatectomy and would leave an inadequate future liver remnant (FLR) if all were removed.  
  • Infiltration of the right portal pedicle represents major vascular involvement, compromising the ability to achieve an R0 resection without complex reconstruction.  
  • Presence of distant metastases (M1) and a high CEA (2500 ng/mL) suggest a high tumor burden, further lowering the likelihood of immediate resectability.  
  • According to current hepatobiliary oncology criteria (e.g., FLR ≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy, and need for negative margins), the case is not resectable at this moment but may become resectable after systemic therapy and/or portal vein modulation.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab for 2–3 months).  
   – Aim: tumor shrinkage of hepatic lesions, possible conversion of vascular invasion, and assessment of tumor biology (CEA trend).  

B. Re‑assessment imaging (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and CT of chest/abdomen) after induction therapy.  
   – Determine response of liver metastases, residual portal pedicle involvement, and calculate FLR volume.  

C. Portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if FLR remains <30 % but sufficient hypertrophy is achievable.  
   – Goal: induce left‑lobe hypertrophy to allow safe right‑ or extended hepatectomy while preserving oncologic margins.  

D. Surgical resection (multidisciplinary timing):  
   – If response is adequate and FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % after chemotherapy), proceed with a staged or combined approach:  
      First stage – resection of the primary colon tumor (right hemicolectomy) either simultaneously with liver surgery if patient condition permits, or as a separate procedure within 2–4 weeks.  
      Second stage – curative liver resection (right hepatectomy or extended right hepatectomy with portal vein reconstruction) aiming for R0 margins.  
   – If disease remains unresectable after maximal down‑staging, transition to best‑supportive systemic therapy or enrollment in clinical trials.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with nine bilobar liver metastases associated with infiltration of the right portal pedicle and a very high CEA (2500 ng/mL) in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer. The combination of extensive bilobar disease and portal pedicle involvement precludes the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (2500 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response and reassess vascular relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate venous outflow preservation or need for reconstruction.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major response occurs with regression of portal pedicle involvement and significant reduction in tumor burden.
• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective and dependent on restoration of clear vascular anatomy.

E. If disease remains extensive
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• If disease remains extensive, consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 61 years old, T3N1M1 rectal tumor, three liver metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII). CEA 680 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: extension to the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Metastases near venous confluence, high surgical risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Three hepatic metastases confined to segments IVa, VI, and VIII meet the numeric criteria for resection (≤4 lesions).  
  • All lesions are technically resectable provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved; however, the lesion(s) abutting the hepatic vein confluence raise concern for loss of major outflow and may limit the volume of safe resection.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but the high CEA (680 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest aggressive biology, warranting a cautious approach.  
  • The MDT notes “high surgical risk,” implying either limited FLR, compromised hepatic function, or comorbidities; these factors shift the case from outright resectable to potentially resectable pending optimization (e.g., portal vein embolization, staged resection).  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
   - Rationale: Down‑size liver lesions, assess tumor biology, and potentially convert borderline cases to safer resection; KRAS‑mutated disease still responds to chemotherapy.  

B. Re‑assessment after systemic therapy  
   - Repeat contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT, obtain volumetric analysis of FLR, and evaluate response of hepatic lesions and rectal primary.  
   - Rationale: Determine whether the hepatic vein confluence involvement has regressed and whether FLR meets ≥30 % (normal liver) or ≥40 % (steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured liver) criteria.  

C. Pre‑operative liver optimization (if FLR insufficient)  
   - Perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches (or left, depending on planned resection) to hypertrophy the future remnant.  
   - Rationale: Augments FLR volume, reduces postoperative liver failure risk, especially important given the lesion near the hepatic vein confluence.  

D. Surgical phase  
   1. Liver resection – Aim for an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection of segments IVa, VI, and VIII with preservation of the hepatic vein outflow; consider a right hepatectomy with middle hepatic vein preservation or a staged “two‑step” approach (e.g., ALPPS) if FLR remains marginal.  
   2. Rectal tumor management – After hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks), proceed with standard rectal cancer treatment: neoadjuvant chemoradiation if not already given, followed by total mesorectal excision (TME).  
   - Rationale: Prioritizing liver surgery addresses the life‑threatening metastatic burden; rectal surgery can be safely delayed given the absence of obstructive symptoms.  

E. Adjuvant therapy  
   - Continue systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively (e.g., 6 months total) and consider targeted agents based on molecular profile.  
   - Rationale: Reduces risk of recurrence, especially in KRAS‑mutated disease.
Reference:

The patient presents with three liver metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII) with MRI showing extension toward the hepatic vein confluence. Although the number of lesions is limited, their proximity to the venous outflow confluence makes a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate hepatic venous drainage technically uncertain. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but only after careful vascular assessment and likely tumor downsizing.

A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (680 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Given the high CEA (680 ng/mL), KRAS mutation, and complex vascular location, initiate 3–6 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Expert vascular restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the hepatic vein confluence.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate venous outflow preservation or need for reconstruction.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If sufficient tumor regression occurs, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Anticipate possible venous reconstruction or complex vascular control.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections, or standard anatomic major hepatectomy with or without vascular reconstruction aiming for R0 margins.

• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
  • Four bilobar liver metastases meet criteria for hepatic clearance if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be achieved.  
  • R0 resection is technically feasible in principle, but the segment VII lesion invades the inferior vena cava (IVC) over >1 cm, which raises the complexity of achieving negative margins and requires vascular reconstruction.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; however, the IVC involvement places the case at the limits of conventional hepatic resection and mandates multidisciplinary vascular input.  
  • Resectability will depend on volumetric FLR assessment, the ability to reconstruct the IVC safely, and the patient’s physiologic reserve.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months  
   - Rationale: Down‑size hepatic lesions, treat occult micrometastases, and provide a biologic test of tumor responsiveness; high CEA suggests aggressive disease.  

B. Restaging with contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen, liver MRI with volumetry, and PET‑CT if not already performed  
   - Rationale: Re‑evaluate number, size, and distribution of metastases; calculate FLR; assess response of the IVC‑invasive lesion; confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Multidisciplinary surgical planning  
   • If FLR ≥30 % (in a normal liver) or ≥40 % (in a steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured liver) is achievable, proceed with portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to augment FLR.  
   • Plan a two‑stage or simultaneous approach:  
        – Stage 1: Right hepatectomy (including segment VII) with en‑bloc IVC resection and reconstruction (using interposition graft or patch) performed by hepatobiliary‑vascular team.  
        – Stage 2 (if staged): Completion left hepatectomy or segmental resections after FLR hypertrophy.  
   • Alternatively, consider ex‑vivo liver resection with autotransplantation if IVC involvement is extensive and in‑situ reconstruction is deemed unsafe.  

D. Primary colon tumor management  
   – Perform oncologic left‑sided colectomy either before liver surgery (if symptomatic or obstructive) or after hepatic resection (if liver surgery is prioritized).  

E. Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of the pre‑operative regimen or switch to maintenance) for at least 6 months  
   – Rationale: Consolidate response, address microscopic residual disease, and improve disease‑free survival.

The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases, including a segment VII lesion invading the IVC over ~1 cm, without reported extrahepatic disease. While the number of lesions is limited, true caval invasion makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unlikely without complex vascular resection/reconstruction and carries high operative risk. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only in a highly selected setting, after tumor downsizing and multidisciplinary vascular assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (900 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.

• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with or without partial IVC resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with vascular surgery is required to assess feasibility of partial IVC resection/reconstruction if needed.

C. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• One or two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• If regression of caval invasion occurs or reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of all lesions.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or graft reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:

- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
  • Five hepatic lesions, including an 8.5 cm central metastasis in segment IVb with bilateral portal vein contact, raise concerns for insufficient future liver remnant (FLR) and technical complexity.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease beyond the primary colon tumor, but the large central lesion and proximity to major vascular structures exceed conventional criteria for immediate one‑stage curative resection.  
  • Current oncologic guidelines consider such cases potentially resectable after down‑staging systemic therapy and/or FLR augmentation (e.g., portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy).

   – Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to achieve tumor shrinkage and assess biological response (CEA trend, radiographic RECIST).

   – Perform contrast‑enhanced MRI or triphasic CT with liver volumetry after induction therapy.  
   – Evaluate FLR volume, residual tumor size, and relationship to portal/hepatic veins.  
   – Rationale: Objective measurement determines feasibility of curative resection and need for hypertrophy strategies.

   – If FLR <30 % (or <40 % after chemotherapy), proceed with portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected, targeting ≥10 % hypertrophy.  
   – After adequate hypertrophy (typically 2–4 weeks), perform a two‑stage hepatectomy:  
        • Stage 1: Resection of peripheral metastases (parenchymal‑sparing) if feasible.  
        • Stage 2: Anatomic right trisectionectomy including segment IVb (or extended left hepatectomy) to remove the central lesion.  
   – Rationale: Staged approach maximizes FLR while achieving R0 resection of all hepatic disease.  

D. Post‑operative systemic therapy and surveillance  
   – Resume adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) for 3–6 months post‑resection.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months.  
   – Rationale: High baseline CEA and aggressive primary tumor warrant systemic control of micrometastatic disease.  

E. Contingency plan (if down‑staging insufficient)  
   – Continue systemic therapy with reassessment; consider liver‑directed modalities (Y‑90 radioembolization, stereotactic body radiotherapy, or percutaneous ablation) for residual lesions.  
   – Evaluate eligibility for clinical trials or palliative care based on response and patient status.

MDT Discussion: Normal CEA despite high volume, question regarding biological sensitivity for follow-up.

- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Only two hepatic metastases, each ≤5 cm, which is within conventional size limits for curative hepatectomy.  
  • Absence of reported extra‑hepatic disease suggests disease confined to liver and primary colon.  
  • RAS‑wild‑type, BRAF‑wild‑type genotype predicts favorable response to modern systemic regimens and does not preclude surgery.  
  • Definitive determination of resectability requires additional data on lesion location (segmental distribution, proximity to major vessels/ biliary structures) and on the anticipated future liver remnant (FLR) relative to the patient’s hepatic functional reserve.

   - Rationale: Provides early treatment of micrometastatic disease, allows assessment of tumor biology (response kinetics), and may downsize lesions to facilitate parenchymal‑sparing resection.

   - Re‑evaluate size and number of metastases.  
   - Map segmental anatomy and calculate FLR.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, left T4N1M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (up to 5.6 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 1400 ng/mL. KRAS G12C mutation confirmed.
MDT Discussion: Specific molecular profile, may benefit from a later targeted strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Six hepatic lesions up to 5.6 cm do not per se preclude resection; modern series report R0 resection with >5 lesions when adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported; absence of peritoneal or pulmonary metastases favors a curative intent.  
  • Resectability hinges on (a) volumetric assessment of FLR (≥20 % in a normal liver, ≥30‑40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), (b) anatomical distribution (unilobar vs bilobar), and (c) ability to achieve negative margins (R0) without compromising vascular inflow/outflow.  
  • The primary tumor is T4N1, indicating locally advanced disease; however, simultaneous or staged colon resection can be incorporated once hepatic disease is down‑staged.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   • Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS G12C mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   • Goal: tumor shrinkage to facilitate R0 liver resection, assess biologic response (CEA trend, radiologic RECIST), and treat occult micrometastases.  

B. Restaging after 2–3 months of chemotherapy  
   • Repeat high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with volumetric analysis of FLR.  
   • Evaluate lesion response, distribution, and any emergence of extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Conversion to surgical resection (plan based on restaging)  
   • If lesions become unilobar or FLR is insufficient, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS to augment FLR.  
   • If adequate FLR (>30 % after chemotherapy) and lesions are amenable to a single‑stage resection, proceed with simultaneous colon resection (segmental colectomy) and liver resection (anatomic or non‑anatomic as dictated by lesion location).  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion margins and detect occult disease.  

D. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   • Resume systemic therapy to complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy.

Man, 57 years old, low T3N2M1 rectal cancer, four peripheral liver metastases (2-3.5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 90 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS, positive circulating tumor cells.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating cells despite low volume, prognostic significance discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is potentially resectable. The liver disease consists of four peripheral metastases, each ≤3.5 cm, without major vascular or biliary involvement, which meets conventional criteria for hepatic resection (≤5 lesions, all amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with a projected future liver remnant ≥30 % in a normal liver). However, resectability cannot be confirmed until volumetric analysis, functional liver reserve, and the ability to achieve an R0 margin for both the hepatic and rectal sites are verified. The presence of circulating tumor cells and high CEA suggest aggressive biology, but do not preclude a curative approach if disease control is achieved with systemic therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (6–8 cycles) – FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status. Rationale: down‑size liver lesions, eradicate micrometastatic disease, and assess tumor biology (response of CTCs/CEA).  

B. Concurrent or sequential neoadjuvant chemoradiation for the rectal primary – Long‑course pelvic radiotherapy (50.4 Gy) with concurrent capecitabine or 5‑FU, followed by a short interval. Rationale: standard of care for T3N2 rectal cancer to achieve local control and potential down‑staging.  

C. Restaging imaging and functional liver assessment – Repeat contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI, liver volumetry, and indocyanine‑green clearance (or similar) after systemic therapy. Rationale: confirm that all hepatic lesions remain resectable, verify FLR adequacy, and document radiologic response.

   • Perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (e.g., two non‑anatomic wedge resections or segmentectomies) aiming for R0 margins.  
   Rationale: addresses the metastatic burden early, reduces risk of progression while the rectal primary is being treated, and allows postoperative recovery before pelvic surgery.  

E. Definitive rectal surgery – Low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection with total mesorectal excision, performed 6–8 weeks after liver resection once the patient has recovered. Rationale: completes curative intent for the primary tumor after systemic disease control.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Resume/continue chemotherapy (e.g., 4–6 cycles) post‑operatively, possibly with maintenance anti‑EGFR if CTCs remain detectable. Rationale: consolidate response, address any residual microscopic disease, and monitor CTC/CEA trends.

Case_Content:
Woman, 68 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥10 lesions) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2700 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Massive liver disease with high marker elevation, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Unresectable at present (potentially convertible).  
- Rationale:  
  • ≥10 hepatic lesions, most likely bilobar, exceed the commonly accepted limit for upfront resection (generally ≤5‑6 lesions or limited to one lobe).  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume; with this tumor burden the FLR would likely be insufficient for safe major hepatectomy.  
  • T4N2 primary tumor and markedly elevated CEA (2700 ng/mL) indicate aggressive biology.  
  • KRAS mutation predicts lower response to anti‑EGFR agents and may limit down‑staging options.  
  • Absence of information on extra‑hepatic disease, performance status, and liver function precludes assuming resectability.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   - Initiate an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) aiming for tumor shrinkage and potential down‑staging of hepatic disease.  
   - Rationale: High tumor burden and aggressive biology require systemic control before any surgical attempt; conversion therapy can reduce lesion number/size and improve FLR feasibility.  

B. Radiologic and functional reassessment after 2–3 cycles  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI and volumetric liver analysis; assess response per RECIST and calculate FLR.  
   - Rationale: Determines whether lesions have become resectable or if portal vein embolization (PVE) is needed to augment FLR.  

C. Consideration of staged hepatic resection (if reassessment shows adequate response)  
   - If sufficient tumor regression and FLR ≥ 30 % (≥40 % in compromised liver), proceed with:  
     • Portal vein embolization or ligation to hypertrophy the future remnant, followed by interval imaging.  
     • Either a single extended hepatectomy or a two‑stage hepatectomy (including possible associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS) based on lesion distribution.  
   - Rationale: Staged approach maximizes curative potential while preserving postoperative liver function.  

D. Continuation of systemic therapy / clinical trial enrollment  
   - If disease remains unresectable after optimal systemic therapy, maintain chemotherapy, consider inclusion in trials (e.g., immunotherapy for MSI‑high if applicable, novel targeted agents), or shift to best supportive care based on patient wishes.  
   - Rationale: Ongoing systemic control is the mainstay for unresectable metastatic colorectal cancer; trial participation may offer additional benefit.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T3N1M1 colon cancer at the abdominal CT scan, three liver metastases (2-3 cm) and confirmed left portal invasion on liver MRI. CEA 310 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Unilateral portal involvement, potentially approachable depending on volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Three hepatic metastases (2‑3 cm) are limited in number and size, meeting conventional criteria for hepatic resection.  
  • Involvement is confined to the left portal vein branch (unilateral), which can be addressed with portal vein embolization (PVE) or staged hepatectomy to induce hypertrophy of the future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • No reported extra‑hepatic disease beyond the primary colon lesion; therefore, a curative intent approach remains feasible.  
  • Definitive resectability hinges on adequate FLR volume (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % after chemotherapy) and the ability to obtain R0 margins after clearing the portal invasion; these parameters are not yet quantified, hence the “potentially” qualifier.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
   - Rationale: Down‑size liver lesions, treat occult micrometastases, assess tumor biology (response, CEA trend).  

B. Restaging imaging and functional assessment (triphasic CT or MRI with volumetry, liver function tests, ICG clearance).  
   - Rationale: Determine response of metastases, re‑evaluate extent of left portal involvement, calculate FLR volume, and confirm hepatic functional reserve.  

C. Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the left portal branch (or right PVE if a right‑sided resection is planned) followed by a 2–4 week interval for hypertrophy.  
   - Rationale: Increase FLR to safe thresholds, making a single‑stage curative hepatectomy possible.  

D. Surgical resection (planned as a right hepatectomy or extended right hepatectomy to include the left portal tributary, with simultaneous or staged resection of the primary colon tumor).  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 margins on both hepatic and colonic disease; a combined approach reduces overall treatment time and aligns with curative intent.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of the pre‑operative regimen or adjustment based on pathology).  
   - Rationale: Consolidate response, address any residual microscopic disease, and improve disease‑free survival.

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, right T3N0M1 colon tumor, single 5.6 cm metastasis in segment VIII, in close contact with IVC at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 540 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis, major technical question regarding surgical approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
   Single hepatic lesion, no documented extra‑hepatic disease, fulfilling the oncologic principle of solitary metastasis.  
   RAS wild‑type status and high CEA suggest biologically aggressive disease but do not preclude resection.  
   Proximity to the inferior vena cava (IVC) represents a technical challenge rather than an absolute contraindication; vascular reconstruction or cavoplasty can achieve an R0 margin if adequate liver remnant can be preserved.  
   Patient age (72 y) alone is not a barrier provided functional reserve is acceptable.  
   Resectability hinges on (a) sufficient future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 40 % in older patients), (b) ability to obtain negative margins without compromising major vascular flow, and (c) absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Perform liver‑specific MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging, contrast‑enhanced CT volumetry, and PET‑CT to confirm solitary disease, delineate exact tumor‑IVC relationship, assess hepatic veins, and calculate FLR.  
   - Rationale: precise anatomic mapping is essential for planning complex vascular resection and for confirming the absence of occult metastases.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (2–3 months)  
   - Regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (or FOLFOX + bevacizumab if tolerance is a concern).  
   - Rationale: down‑size the lesion away from the IVC, treat micrometastatic disease, and provide a biological test of tumor responsiveness; high baseline CEA predicts benefit from systemic therapy.  

C. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat MRI/CT volumetry and PET‑CT.  
   - Evaluate tumor shrinkage, change in IVC contact, FLR adequacy, and any new lesions.  
   - Rationale: decision point for proceeding to surgery versus alternative approaches.  

D. Surgical intervention (if R0 achievable)  
   - Planned procedure: extended right hepatectomy or segment VIII‑centric anatomical resection with en‑bloc partial IVC resection and primary patch repair or interposition graft (e.g., PTFE or autologous pericardial patch).  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins and vascular anatomy.  
   - Ensure FLR > 40 % (consider portal vein embolization pre‑operatively if FLR borderline).  
   - Rationale: achieve negative margins while preserving sufficient functional liver; vascular reconstruction is feasible in experienced centers.  

E. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months; consider adding anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status.  
   - Rationale: eradicate residual microscopic disease and reduce recurrence risk.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 5.6 cm liver metastasis in segment VIII in close contact with the IVC, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although solitary, the central location and caval proximity make a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection technically demanding and potentially unsafe without prior tumor downsizing or vascular planning. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but only after careful vascular assessment and likely induction therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of the lesion with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (540 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and hepatic veins.
• If regression occurs or vascular control is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or reconstruction with multidisciplinary discussion with vascular surgery to assess feasibility of tangential IVC resection if needed.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Management of primary tumor
• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
  • Six hepatic lesions ranging 1.5‑4 cm involve both lobes (bilobar disease), which challenges a single‑stage anatomic resection but does not automatically preclude surgery if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be achieved.  
  • No information on FLR volume, hepatic functional reserve, or vascular involvement; these are essential to confirm technical resectability.  
  • BRAF V600E mutation and markedly elevated CEA (850 ng/mL) indicate aggressive tumor biology and high systemic risk, but they do not by themselves make hepatic resection impossible; they do, however, lower the likelihood of durable cure without systemic disease control.  
  • Age 69 and presumed good performance status (not stated) are not absolute contraindications.

A. Initiate systemic conversion therapy  
   - Regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab, with addition of a BRAF‑targeted combination (encorafenib + cetuximab) if tolerated.

   - Rationale: Prioritize control of life‑threatening disease while preserving the opportunity for curative‑intent hepatic resection.

Case_Content:
Woman, 65 years old, T4N1M1 rectal tumor, four liver metastases at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Immuno-sensitive profile, discussion on optimal therapeutic sequence.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Four hepatic lesions are present; resectability depends on their size, lobar distribution, and relationship to major vascular structures, which are not detailed.  
  • No explicit evidence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the primary rectal tumor; therefore, liver‑only metastatic burden can be addressed surgically if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved (≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy).  
  • The primary tumor is T4N1, indicating locally advanced disease that will require neoadjuvant treatment before definitive resection, but this does not preclude eventual hepatic resection.  
  • RAS wild‑type and MSI‑H status do not affect technical resectability but influence systemic therapy choice.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Initiate systemic therapy with pembrolizumab (PD‑1 inhibitor) as first‑line for MSI‑H metastatic colorectal cancer, optionally combined with a fluoropyrimidine‑based regimen (e.g., FOLFOX) to enhance tumor shrinkage of liver lesions.  
   – Rationale: MSI‑H tumors respond dramatically to immunotherapy; concurrent chemotherapy can improve response of bulky hepatic disease.  

B. After 8–12 weeks, perform restaging with high‑resolution liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted imaging) and a PET‑CT to assess response of hepatic lesions and to delineate exact anatomical distribution.  
   – Rationale: Precise mapping is essential to determine whether a single‑stage hepatectomy, two‑stage approach, or portal vein embolization (PVE) is required.  

C. Treat the rectal primary with long‑course chemoradiation (45–50 Gy with concurrent capecitabine or 5‑FU) followed by a 6‑8‑week interval.  
   – Rationale: T4 disease mandates down‑staging to achieve an R0 mesorectal excision and to reduce the risk of local recurrence.  

D. Re‑evaluate resectability after chemoradiation and systemic therapy response:  
   – If all liver lesions can be cleared with an adequate FLR, proceed to simultaneous or staged liver resection (preferably staged after completion of rectal surgery if the FLR is sufficient).  
   – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization or a two‑stage hepatectomy (including possible ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy before definitive liver resection.  
   – Rationale: Achieving R0 hepatic margins while preserving liver function is paramount; staged approaches allow safe hypertrophy and reduce postoperative liver failure risk.  

E. Perform definitive rectal surgery (total mesorectal excision) after completion of neoadjuvant therapy and once hepatic disease is controlled, unless a simultaneous approach is deemed safe based on operative risk and FLR.  
   – Rationale: Ensures oncologically sound removal of the primary tumor and allows coordinated postoperative recovery.  

F. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy as indicated by pathology (e.g., continuation of immunotherapy if residual disease or high‑risk features).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four liver metastases in the setting of a T4N1 rectal tumor. Although the liver disease may be technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection, the MSI-H profile indicates a high likelihood of major response to immunotherapy. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is potentially resectable, but surgery is not the first step given the expected efficacy of systemic immunotherapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 4 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

B. First-line systemic immunotherapy (mandatory)
• Initiate immunotherapy according to MDT decision as first-line treatment for MSI-H metastatic colorectal cancer.
• The objective is major tumor regression and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical re-evaluation after response
• If a major radiologic response occurs, reassess segmental resectability.
