Case_Content:
Man, 60 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1300 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: contact with right hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular invasion, significant operative risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Eight bilobar metastases exceed the typical criteria for upfront single‑stage resection (generally ≤4 lesions confined to one lobe or ≤2 lesions per lobe with adequate FLR).  
  • Contact with the right hepatic vein indicates possible major vascular involvement, raising the risk of insufficient venous outflow after resection.  
  • Superior vascular invasion (presumed involvement of hepatic veins or IVC) further limits the ability to achieve an R0 liver resection in a single operation.  
  • The patient’s high operative risk (unspecified but noted) and the need to preserve an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) make immediate curative hepatectomy unsafe.  
  • However, no extra‑hepatic disease other than the primary colon tumor is reported, and systemic therapy may downsize lesions, allowing a staged or hypertrophy‑based approach; therefore the case is not categorically unresectable.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to attempt tumor downstaging and assess biologic response (CEA trend, imaging).  
   - Rationale: KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents; high tumor burden and CEA suggest aggressive disease that may respond to triplet regimen, potentially converting lesions to resectable status.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Perform repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and volumetric CT to evaluate lesion response, vascular involvement, and calculate FLR volume.  
   - Obtain liver function tests (bilirubin, ICG clearance, ALBI score) and assess performance status (ECOG).  
   - Rationale: Determines whether sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR exist to proceed with curative surgery or if further downstaging is needed.  

C. Hypertrophy‑inducing strategy (if FLR inadequate)  
   - If FLR <30 % (or <40 % in a cirrhotic liver) after response assessment, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the diseased lobe or consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) in a high‑volume center.  
   - Rationale: Increases future liver remnant to safe levels, enabling major hepatectomy while preserving oncologic margins.  

D. Surgical resection  
   - Option 1: Two‑stage hepatectomy – First stage: resect lesions in the future liver remnant (typically left lobe) plus PVE of right lobe; second stage (6–8 weeks later) – right hepatectomy after hypertrophy.  
   - Option 2: Single‑stage extended right hepatectomy – If post‑therapy imaging shows clearance of right hepatic vein involvement and FLR is adequate, proceed with an anatomic right trisectionectomy with venous reconstruction as needed.  
   - Simultaneous or delayed resection of the primary colon tumor based on symptomatology and oncologic timing (often delayed after liver clearance to reduce postoperative morbidity).  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 resection of all hepatic disease while maintaining sufficient liver function; timing of primary tumor resection balances surgical risk and disease control.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Resume or continue systemic therapy post‑hepatectomy (e.g., capecitabine‑oxaliplatin) for 3–6 months, tailored to response and tolerability.  
   - Rationale: Reduces risk of recurrence given initial high tumor burden and KRAS‑mutated biology.

   – Rationale: Achieve R0 resection while preserving adequate liver function.

Man, 62 years old, T3N1M1 upper rectal tumor, liver metastases (3-5 cm) with contact with IVC and right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 580 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Complex central metastases, discussion on combined approach or venous reconstruction.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Liver lesions are 3‑5 cm, centrally located but appear confined to the right hepatic territory with contact to the inferior vena cava (IVC) and right hepatic vein (RHV).  
  • No radiologic evidence of distant extra‑hepatic disease beyond the primary rectal tumor.  
  • Current hepatobiliary criteria consider lesions involving major vascular structures resectable if vascular reconstruction is feasible and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • The need for IVC/RHV reconstruction places the case in the “potentially resectable” category pending assessment of FLR volume, hepatic inflow/outflow, and patient’s operative risk.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab)  
   - Rationale: Down‑size hepatic metastases, assess tumor biology, and potentially convert marginal vascular involvement to resectable margins; also treat micrometastatic disease.  
B. Restaging with high‑resolution multiphase CT or MRI and volumetric analysis of FLR after systemic therapy  
   - Rationale: Determine response, re‑evaluate vascular involvement, and calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % of total liver volume, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS).  
C. Surgical phase (performed after adequate FLR is secured)  
   • Option 1: One‑stage right hepatectomy with en bloc IVC and RHV resection and reconstruction using prosthetic graft or autologous conduit, followed by immediate rectal resection (if patient fit).  
   • Option 2: Staged approach – first liver resection with vascular reconstruction, then, after recovery (4–6 weeks), low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection of the rectal primary.  
   - Rationale: Central hepatic disease mandates vascular control; simultaneous colorectal resection is considered only if operative time and physiological stress are acceptable.  
D. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy (e.g., continuation of systemic chemotherapy ± targeted agents) and surveillance (CEA, imaging every 3–6 months).  
   - Rationale: High baseline CEA and aggressive biology warrant adjuvant treatment to reduce recurrence risk.

   - Rationale: Early detection of recurrence for timely intervention.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

G. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Three hepatic metastases meet the numeric criteria for resection, and no extra‑hepatic disease is reported.  
  • RAS wild‑type status and MSS phenotype support the possibility of effective systemic down‑staging.  
  • Invasion of the hepatic vein confluence represents major vascular involvement, raising technical complexity and risk of insufficient future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • The MDT notes “significant technical risk” and the need for volumetric assessment, indicating that resection is not outright feasible without further evaluation (e.g., FLR calculation, possible portal vein embolization or staged approach).

A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate an intensive chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status.

   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT volumetry to quantify FLR and delineate the relationship of metastases to hepatic veins.

   - Plan an anatomic extended right hepatectomy (or right trisectionectomy) with possible hepatic vein reconstruction (e.g., interpositional graft) or parenchymal‑sparing resections if lesions allow.  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 resection of all hepatic disease while preserving sufficient functional liver tissue; vascular reconstruction addresses the confluence involvement.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume adjuvant systemic therapy tailored to response and tolerability; monitor CEA and imaging per standard surveillance schedule.

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Four hepatic metastases, each 3‑5 cm, located bilaterally → multiple, sizable lesions in both lobes reduce the likelihood of a single‑stage anatomic resection with adequate future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • No reported extra‑hepatic disease beyond the colon primary, but the presence of bilobar disease places the case at the upper limit of resectability criteria.  
  • The atypical BRAF D594G mutation confers an intermediate prognosis; patients with this genotype can benefit from conversion chemotherapy to achieve sufficient tumor shrinkage and improve FLR.  
  • Absence of data on FLR volume, liver function, and vascular involvement precludes labeling the case as outright resectable; therefore it remains potentially resectable pending down‑staging and volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (8‑12 weeks)  
   – Regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (or anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type) tailored to BRAF D594G biology.  
   – Rationale: Aim for tumor shrinkage, conversion to resectability, and early treatment of micrometastatic disease.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment (4‑6 weeks after chemotherapy)  
   – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or PET‑CT to evaluate response, lesion size, and distribution.  
   – Volumetric CT to calculate FLR; consider ICG clearance or liver function tests.  
   – Rationale: Determine whether a single‑stage resection is feasible or if a staged approach (two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS) is required.  

C. Surgical planning based on restaging  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (normal liver) or ≥ 40 % (steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured liver) and lesions are amenable to clear margins: proceed to simultaneous colon resection and hepatectomy (segmental/partial resections preserving parenchyma).  
   • If FLR insufficient or lesions remain bilobar despite response: plan a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in one lobe + portal vein embolization of the contralateral lobe; second stage: resection of the cleared lobe after hypertrophy).  
   – Rationale: Achieve R0 resection while preserving adequate liver function.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy and surveillance  
   – Resume systemic therapy post‑operatively (e.g., continuation of bevacizumab or switch to maintenance capecitabine/oxaliplatin).  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years.  
   – Rationale: Reduce recurrence risk and detect early disease progression.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Six hepatic metastases measuring 2‑4 cm each fall within the size range that can be cleared surgically, provided they are not encasing major vascular structures and are amenable to an adequate future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease, which satisfies the primary criterion for hepatic‑only disease.  
  • RAS wild‑type status and absence of KRAS/NRAS mutation favor responsiveness to systemic therapy, increasing the likelihood of conversion to resectability.  
  • The presence of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) indicates biologic aggressiveness but does not, by itself, preclude resection; it underscores the need for systemic therapy before surgery.  
  • Definitive assessment of resectability requires detailed volumetric analysis and anatomic mapping of lesion distribution (unilobar vs bilobar) and proximity to portal/hepatic veins, which are not provided.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging – Obtain liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, volumetric CT for FLR calculation, and whole‑body PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   • Rationale: Precise anatomic detail and functional liver reserve are essential to plan a safe hepatectomy and to confirm true hepatic‑only disease.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – Initiate 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (or FOLFOX + bevacizumab if toxicity concerns).  
   • Rationale: High CEA and CTC positivity suggest micrometastatic burden; intensive chemotherapy aims to downsize lesions, eradicate occult disease, and test tumor biology.  

C. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy – Repeat liver MRI and volumetry; evaluate tumor response (RECIST) and FLR (target >30 % in normal liver, >40 % after chemotherapy).  
   • Rationale: Determines whether a single‑stage resection is feasible or if a staged approach (portal vein embolization, two‑stage hepatectomy, or ALPPS) is required.  

D. Surgical intervention –  
   • If lesions are confined to one lobe and FLR is adequate: proceed with a single‑stage anatomic or non‑anatomic hepatectomy achieving R0 margins.  
   • If bilobar disease or insufficient FLR: consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in the future liver remnant, portal vein embolization of the diseased lobe; second stage: resection of the embolized lobe) or ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy is needed.  
   • Simultaneous or staged resection of the primary colon tumor: perform a segmental colectomy either during the same operative session (if operative time and patient condition allow) or within 4–6 weeks after hepatic surgery.  
   • Rationale: Achieving complete (R0) removal of all macroscopic disease offers the best chance for long‑term survival; staged liver surgery preserves hepatic function.  

E. Adjuvant/continuation systemic therapy – Complete a total of 12 cycles of chemotherapy (including neoadjuvant and postoperative courses) and consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab) if further molecular profiling supports benefit.  
   • Rationale: Consolidates response, addresses residual microscopic disease, and mitigates risk of recurrence, especially given initial high CTC burden.
